"PAPA, what is that picture over the mantel-piece" The vain father answered, "Why that's papa's arts, my darling 1"—" Then why don't you have your legs put up too," was the reply. A GENTLEMAN in one of the steam-boats asked the steward, when he came round to collect the passage-money (Is. each for the best cabin), if there was no danger of being blowy& up? The steward promptly replied—" No, air, not the least; we can- not afford to blow up at these low prices." THE person who has not been a grandmother knows nothing of the anxieties of this life. It is bad enough to have a drunken husband, but when you come to compare that affliction with two generations of croup, hooping cough, and measles, you elevate a sprained ankle to the dignity of a broken leg, and class toothaches with apple-plexy.

She looked pale on discovering her loss the next day. I have a great objection to hirus." Betty curtsied, withdrew, and took the hint.

div.head: WHAT A BLIND MAN DID.
div.p: WHAT A BLIND MAN DID.

Of the many stories on record of the accomplish- ments of men thtally blind, I regard the following as one of the most remarkable. I find it in the report of a commission whose only aim in what they gave to the public was to present a record of facts.

_ John Metcalf was a native of the West Riding of Yorkshire, born in the year 1717, only a few miles from Harrowgate. He lost his sight, from the effects of the measles, when four years old, and very shortly became totally blind—utterly unconscious of light 1 His first efforts towards sustaining him- self were made upom the violin. He became an expert performer on the instrument when a mere boy, and for many years attended as a musician at the Queen's Head, in High Harrogate. At the age of five-and-twenty he had saved money enough with which to purchase a wheeled carriage and horses, for the conveying of people to and from places of public amusement. A few years later he sold his horses, and enlisted to. serve as a musician in COL Thornton's Volun- teers, and was taken prisoner at the battle of Fal- kirk. He was soon released, however, and returned to Knaresborough;" where he was born, and com- menced the busines as a common carrier between that town and York, a distance of sixteen miles

and while thus engaged, he served as guide at night, through the intricate passes, or when the tracks were covered with show. As might he expected, strangers • often hesitated about placing themselves under the guidance of a man so utterly blind that even the glare of the sunlight upon the snow was not per- ceptible to him; but he never failed them. Over

_ the trackless waste he would conduct the traveller, where as far as the eye could reach, only a sheet of unbroken and unmarked snow lay upon the earth, and he never went wrong—never hesitated. But,—more than this: When at the age of Potty, he could follow the chase as well and as keenly as the best. He had his own hounds and his own horses, and he could follow those hounds as surely as the the keenest-sighted man of the county. Later in life—but in his prime—he was engaged in a business which it would seem impossible that a blind man could follow. But, incredible as it

may appear, it nevertheless was so. The business was that of projecting and contracting for the making of high roads; building bridges and.houses, and other works of like character. With no other assistance than that of a long stalfin his hand, he would ascend the precipice, explore the valley. investigate thoroughly, and so determine heights, depts, geography, and all thing requisite for him to know. The plans which he made, and the estimates, were done in a manner peculiarly his own, which he could not explain, understandingly to others. John Metcalf was on a visit to his native place in the year 1788, boing then seventy-one years of age—healthy, rugged, and strong. He had come from Huddersfield, in Yorkshire, where he had just finished the building of a piece of road, and the construction of a splendid bridge.

A STORY IS told of the late Lord Clarendon, who entered on one occasion a restaurant in Paris to dine as a simple trader. Having ordered a frugal meal, he called for a 'bottle of champaigne. The waiter, anticipating that the customer might not be able to settle, whispered that the price wes twenty- five francs a bottle, in the hope of "mating an end to his lordship's extravagance. "Oh, in that case." said the earl. 'bring me two bottles."

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

The French papers of the day after the Royal wedding have afforded plenty of amusement to English readers of the telegraphic despatches of the ceremony. The references to "Buckingham," with- out it being considered necessary to mention the Palace, and Marlborough "Hall," are trivial when compared with Cheapseake,Fall-moun (sic), Hill-st., Midgare, and West-sud, whichOt must be confessed, are utterly puzzling. Templus Bar,even the average London cabman might understand. It is pleasant to note that the correspondents are all agreed in their admiration of the orderly character of our Englis!, crowds and the good humour of the police, which certainly offers a curious contrast to the behaviour of their colleagues on the banks of the Seine jest at present.

Mr. Mackinley, who ,died at Melbourne, on Satur- day,was taken ill whilst his wife,Madame Sterling, was giving a series ot concerts in that city, and he was unable to accompany his wife to New Zealand, where she now is. The deceased gentleman was a wealthy American,who followed the singer to Eng- land when shelirst came here as Miss Sterling. lie sk as a.thorough musician, and to him is due much of Madame Sterling's success, on account not only of his excellent business ability,but of his unerring judgment in the selection of the songs which are popularly identified with Madame Sterling's name. the circumstances of his death are particularly sad, , as not only was his devoted wife in New Zealand, but his children are in London under the care of friends.

The Queen is an ardent lover of photography as a means of preserving memories of past events, whether it be a stately pageant at St. James's or a holiday incident in the lonely reaches of the Dee. She is, of course, not herself an operator, but every facility exists in the royal homes for the develop- ment of the hobby, and alp possession of a camera on the part of a member of the Household, as in the case of Lord de Hos, is a special passport to the Queen's favour. The number of scrap albums pos- sessed by her Majesty is ehdless, and some of them are taken with her, whenever the location of the Court is changed. But there are supplies also en permanence at each palace, many of them being unique copies, as the negatives are frequently des- troyed as soon as a good impression is taken. Should an amateur succeed in taking a really good view of any place in which she is interested, the Queen never declines a copy of it.

Mr. Henniker Heaton, M.P., who is talked about as the leader of the Conservative wing of the Australian party in the House, possesses, at his comfortable establishment in Eaton-rquare,a unique souvenir of his public career. There are few men in the House ot Commons who have been the sub- ject of b 0 much good-humoured ridicule and satire throughout the long years of his devotion to the un- romantic subject of postal facilities, and Mr. Henniker lit aton's souvenir consists of a collection of all the cartoons squibs, satirical verses, carica- tures, abuse, ridicule, and anonymous letters with which he has been visited, that is, so far as they have come under his notice. His pet. hobby seems to have given as much food to the journalistic 'numourists as if he had been a Prime Minister or a leader of the Temperance party.

Mrs. Viztoria Woodhull Martin has added the " humanitarian " to the list of sixpenny monthly magazines, and its appearance signalises her return to the active occupation of public lecturer. Of course, both the magazine and the lectures Will deal with the subject—that of scientific propagation— which Mrs. Martin has elevated into a religion. She is certainly one of the most remarkable ot liv- ing lady reformers. When Mrs. Martin, then Victoria Woodhull, began expounding her views on the physical regeneration of the human race, the subject was regarded as one which no respectable person should discuss. Together with her sister, the present Lady Cook, she was persecuted, slan- dered, abused, and even imprisoned. But Mrs. Martin persevered, and not only founded a school of scientific thought, but also laid the foundations of a literature, the evidence of which is seen every month in our brightest magazines and reviews. At the present time many of the first thinkers of the age in problems of moral and scientific progress may be met at 17, Hyde Park-gate, the beautiful home of the woman who, years ago, was mercilessly hounded both by science and society.

Of sweet, amiable presence, endow d with per- sonal charms which seems to disarm tin. ',Mrs. Mar- tin is nevertheless a born reformer. In 1870, in com- pany with her sister, she gave a startling turn to the female emancipation movement by setting up as a banker and broker in IVall-st., New York, and every newspaper in America set itself the task of chronicling the doings of what they called •• the Queens of Finance." Mrs. Martin's idea was to show that women are capable of qualifying themselves for onerous and intricate businesses, and also that business can be conducted with clean hands and truthful tongues.

Another famous exploit of Mrs. Martin was to fight the United States Congress on the point bat under the Constitution every woman citizen of the States was entitled to a vote, and before Congress had decided against her some of the great legal luminaries of America were on her side. After that ehe was nominated as a candidate for the Presidency of the States ; and we inly expect, on her return to public life after so many years of hard but quiet work at home, that she will once again, step into the foremost rank of the women workers of the day.

div.head: OUTBREAK OF DISEASE.
div.p: OUTBREAK OF DISEASE.

The Medical Officer reported that lie had examined the premises occupied by Dr. Ormsby, at Halton, and had lound a series of sanitary defects,whieh in the aggregate constituted a nuisance dangerous and injuriousto health. Four ca..es of typhoid fever had occurred on a farm at Weston. The cases appeared to be mild. The disease was attributed to the well water, but as the use of this was discontinued and Runcorn watrr being laid on for the house, no further action was called for. A case of cholera had been reported from Weston,but an investiga- tion showed that it was only what was known as Eng- lish cholera, or a severe form of diarrlacea, and no action was called for. A case of diptheria was reported from Aston, no action called for. A ease of typhoid fever had occurred at the Limes, Whitley superior. No sanitary defects were found. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Aaron that in future the medical officer be em- powered to tike samples of water whenever he thought it necessary.

div.head: FREE FROM SMALLPDX.
div.p: FREE FROM SMALLPDX.

It was recorded on the minutes of the Smallpox Com- mittee that the district was free from the disease. The Comniittee decided to pay a Ina n named Ecclestiall, who had assisted at the hospital, £4 for the services he had rendered. It was resolved to terminate the engagement of Miss Orion on the 14th inst. Mr.and Mrs.Eccleshall were appointed to the charge of the hospital, and to perform such duties as the Authority might require, at a salary of 30s. per week with coals provided tor them. It was also decided thcit the appointment of Dr. Adams be de- termined at the end of a month.—The report was adopted on the motion of Ur. Williams.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NELLIE, Nothing is really more becomint to a girlish face than white, and (although it certainly soils quickly) if substantial materials are chosen it washes well, ,which is more than can be said for many , decided tints. The, only exception to the veto which seems laid on white washing gowns is in favour of skirts and open-frouted coats of drill, which are much worn with coloured blouses or stiff-fronted shirts, and very nice they look if the skirt is well-shaped, as, the material being rather stiff, it is apt to hang badly if at all awkwardly out. A pretty costume for a fair girl consists of a skirt and coat of white drill with-a cross-over blouse of pale blue cotton, the costume being com- pleted by a big black straw bat, trimmed. with bows of white guipure and bundles of pale blue forget-me-nots. -This is really a most useful as well as smart style of dress, and if the coat is not made too tight at first, it may be washed over and over again without the least detriment to its appear- &nee.

A very dainty bonnet is of deck green velvet, trimmed with black jet and a bow of rich black 'Win ribbon, with jet osprey. A large cut jet star ple.ced on the centre of the crown, and out jet heads, the size of a pea, are set close together the whole way round the edge of the bonnet, which is finished by narrow strings and a small made-up bow. This takes a yard and a quarter of inch-wide green ribbon velvet. I hope you will remember that a made.up bow is better in every• way thaa one tied. It lasts treble as long, and always looks nice, besides saving valuable time when dressing in. haste. '

Both jackets and capes are much worn this summer, and the most fashionable little capes are now built of black moir6 antique trimmed with "roussie," or ecru entredeux. They are formed of three superposed capes,, or one single pelerine, reaching just to the waist, while over the shoulders an original collar-like arrangement of Chiffon and lace gives a light and effective appearance to a smart, and, at the same time, useful wrap. I have an idea that during the autumn days an old fashion will be revived, i.e., that of rather long peau de soie or black satin jackets. I have seen one model of the first-named material, lined throughout with pale blue satin. It reached nearly to the knees, and was made to fasten across the chest with one handsome strass button when worn closed. When open, it showed guipure entredeux on the blue lining of the fronts, met by a volumin- ous collar of peau de soie, edged with entredeux to match, and forming pelerine at the back. On the shoulders it fell in picturesque flutes or folds, and completed a very neat and chic mantle. The skirt of the jacket was rather full, and set in at the back in a series of fan-like pleats.

A very net article of attire, and one which is very fashionable this season, is a white shirt, with quite a stiff front, embroidered all over with tiny sprays of flowers. These shirts are sold at 2s. 9d., and can be obtained either in all white or with embroideries of vale p:nlc, pale blue, or heliotrope. Hollands and coloured linens are still very fashionable, and a pretty brown holland dress I noticed last week was trimmed in a most uncom- mon way with Inds and pipings of pink and white batiste. The newest way of making them up is with e, bodice that has a long, full, all-round basque which quite meets in front, the bodice fronts, however, being cut off above the waist, showing a shirt or blouse beneath. A wide waist- band, either of the material or of stout ribbon, passes round the waist over the coat, and to this band the front parts of the basque are sewn. Striped galatea or shirting looks well made up in this way, as do red and white, or blue and ishite striped flannels with belts and vests of rod or bine, according to the colour of the stripe.

A dainty gown is of white muslin. The skirt is arranged with tiny flounces of muslin, edged with eatin ribbon and fine lace. The bodice is prettily trimmed to correspond. If before leaving for your holidays you would like to provide yourself with some smart and pretty hats and bonnets at nominal prices, you can obtain them now, as many of the caterers for fashion are now commencing their summer sales. A charming hat was of coarse open-work straw, in the fashion- able shape, turned right up from the face in front, with a large bow ot satin ribbon and sprays of flowers, and I was astonished to hear that the price for this lovely hat was only half a guinea. For similar sums there are a large hat of cream tuscan straw, the sole trimming consisting of exquisite roses in various shades of pink and crimson, a dainty little jet bonnet, with a butterfly bow of pink accordeon-pleated chiffon, edged with black lace at the back, and one pink rose in "front, an equally pretty bonnet of white guipure edged with jet, and trimmed at tho back with jetted sprays, and a lovely hat, the latest novelty from Paris cf line white straw, the brim covered with a ruin of wilits chiffon edged with tinsel. It was further trimmed with a spray of shaded pink roses, and at the Lack with ostrich tips. Yours sincerely, JENNIE.

div.head: Strawberry Jam.
div.p: Strawberry Jam.

Take tlb crushed sugar to every pound of fruit, sugar not too fine. The fruit should be boiled on a not too erce fire, till it begins to get thick; add sugar; must be watched whilst boiling. Scr 'pa the bottom of thg pan with a wooden spoon to prevent sticking. Skim from time to time, pace in jars, cover with thin pieces of paper soaked in brandy, toucking jam ; cover over top with stiff piece of paper, moisten rim of jar with beaten white Gregg to exclude air, and tie paper round with thin piece of string.

div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDA Y, JULY 15, 1893. DARK WOOD.
Washing Dlew Blankets.

Press the blankets through two or three lathers (a cup- ful of soap jelly made without soda is the best) in which a handful or borax has been dissolved. Water should be pleasantly warm to the hands. ' Move up and down in the suds, squeeze and press against the sides of tub until the blankets look quite cleau. If the lathers are in separate tubs, they will wash two or three blankets, but it is necessary that the water 'should be clean or the colour of the blankets will be spoiled. Rinse in warm water. On no account wring tightly, it would spoil the nap. Shake well and hang straight on line; shake and pull several times whilst drying to raise nap. Air before a good fire for some hours after dry.

div.head: How to Stain Floors.
div.p: How to Stain Floors.

(1). Put an ounce of permanganate of potash into a gallon of water; when thoroughly dissolved, apply with a small Whitewash brush. Put on coat after coat Until is a warm dark brown, then, when thoroughly dry, polish with a beeswax and turpentine. (2). Add Just enough copperas to strong lye, made from wood ashes, to give it an oak shade, and, when dry, varnish the boards ; or, a floor may be oiled with boiled linseed oil, applied with a paint brush, and varnished, and have the same effect, only that it will not change the colour of the wood so much. To clean a stained or oiled floor use soft cloths •and tepid water.

Good Wives. The following were taken from the" Common Place Book of Epigrams," 1825 : Good wives to snails should be akin, Always their houses keep within, But not to carry (fashion hacks !) All they are worth upon their backs, Good wives, like echoes, still should do, Speak but when tbey'le spoken to; But not like echoes, most absurd, To have for ever the, last word. Good wives, like city clocks, should chime, Be regular, and keep in time ; But not, like city clocks, alcud, Be heard by all the vulgar crowd,

A CuriousnWeddina Custom. The Mandingoes, who. inhabit' a tract of country in Africa, are, says the " Ladies Some Journal,'! strict Mahommedans ill religion, but, curiously enough, they Still retain many of the superstitions ot the negro races from which they sprung. Consequently their marriage ceremony is a mixture of,. the two, and, although it is performed by a marbout- or holy man in the mosque, it contains one very ridiculous element. Next in impor- tance to the marbout is the bridegroom's sister, and when the marriage ceremony reaches the point where the visible bond is usually typified in civilization by the ring, this sister steps forward, and in place of the ring presents the lady with a pair of trousers, which are im- mediately donned. The ceremony is concluded by a very mournful song sung by the companions of the bride, who then coaduct her again to the home of her parents, as, owing to the extreme probability of one oz the other retracting at any moment by reason of an unfavourable omen, no house is built until the ceremony is completed. Polygamy is the rule, but each wife. has her own house to keep her from quarrelling with the other wives. They are the mast tyrannical wives in Africa, and, hating each other, band together against their husbands and rule him with a rod of iron.

div.head: MY WATCH AND OTHER WATCHES.
div.p: MY WATCH AND OTHER WATCHES.

One evening last summer I had some writing to do at my house. The weather was very hot, and I took off my coat and waistcoat. My new gold watch (that I had paid £3O for) I laid before me on the table, where I could keep an eye on it. So far so good. I wrote on, and papers accummulated on the table, one of them covering my watch. Reaching out for something I wanted, my arm accidentally swept it to the floor. Oh, heavens, what luck ! I picked it up—tenderly as one picks up a child who has had a bad tumble. Was it still running ? Yes, faintly ; but as I put it to my ear it ticked a few times, feebly and slowly, and then stopped—a dead watch. A minute ago it was a vital thing—now merely a lot of motionless wheels in a case. What was broken ? I couldn't say. The watchmaker must repair it and return it with [ha bill. So much for my stupid carelessness.
Yet nobody is so poor as not to carry a mere valuable watch than that ; one that will run many years without winding. But when it stops, ah ! then, who is able to set it going again ?

Speaking about the one he ownes, Mr. George W. Burton of Kirton Dohne, Boston, says " My heat flut- tered in a way to alarm me. Sometimes it was so bad fancied I could hear it stop beatiny." What ailed Mr. Burton's heart ? Perhaps his letter will help us to find out. He says :—" In October, 1887, I began to feel weary and languid. I had a bad taste in the mouth, and in the morning my teeth and gums were covered with a thick bloody slime. My appetite tailed, ;Ind after eating I had great pain in the chest and stomach. All the time I had a craving for food,but dare not tsk2 solids. It seemed sometimes that my head would burst with pain, and I was FO dizzy I could hardly see. After a while a cough set in, and I spat up great quantities of phlegm. Later on my breathing became very bad, and I would break out in a cold sweat. I kept on growing weaker until it was all 1 could do to get about, and in this condition I con- tinued for four years. During this time I consulted doctors and used all the different medicines I heard of, but none of them did any good."

Now, let's think a minute. Mr. Burton says his heart fluttered and palpitated, he had a hacking cough, and difficulty in breathing—three frightful things. A man might die of any one of them, as we all know. Yet he recovered from all of them—and all at the same time. He says :

". In February, 1891, I heard of what Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup had done In similar cases, and I deter- mined to try it, and got a bottle from Messrs. Grimble and Kent, Chemists, Boston. The first few doses cave relief, and by continuing to use it in a short time I was perfectly cured. I make this statement in order that others may know where to look for a remedy in an ill- ness like mine."
(Signed) "Go. W. BURTON."

! We rejoice at his restoration to inalth, but what, after . all, ailed him? Did he have three diseases—viz., heart cotnplamt, consumption, and asthma ? And, if so, how on earth could Mother Seigel'a Curative Syrup have cured them—each affecting different organs ? The answer is, he had but see disease, indigestion and dyspepsia, of which the feeble heart,the irritated throat, and the burdened lungs were tell-tales and symptoms. The poisoned blood—tilled with deadly acids from the stomach—half paralysed the nerves and thus disordered the heart's action; it also infected the delicate membrane lining of the lungs and air passages, producing asthma and the cough that seamed to threaten consumption. One disease, many misleading symptoms—that is the truth ; deluding physicians, and frightening patients into thinking there is no hope. When life's timepiece runs down no wAwer on earth can wind it up again, but Mr. Burton's C4Se at:d thou- sands more, prove, that it is often good for many a year after you thought the works would soon be motionless in the case.

div.head: REMARKABLE CHARGE BY JUDGE
div.p: REMARKABLE CHARGE BY JUDGE
Gr RA.NTiIAM.
TFIE POLICE STRONGLY CENSURED.

• Addressing the grand jury at the Kent Assizes on Monday, Mr. Justice Grantham referred to the charge of Wife murder preferred against Noel, of Itamsgate. Ti- mid be had read through the evidence taken during the magisterial inquiry; and could not find enough evidenee to cover a singiu piece of papal% It was for the jury to say whether there was a prinut facie case,b»t he thought it impossible for them to make head or tail of it. Ni-vi in his whole experience had he found in one CdSe so much incompetence or illegality on behalf of the prc- secution. The conduct ot Inspector Ross wins strongly criticised. It was not the duty of is constable to act as a badly-bred bloodhound. His lordship intimated that even though a truNtall was found, he should not allow the prisoner to be convicted. The depositions were I wer. laden with rubbish. Evidence which should never have been admitted was given • that which ou.„:ht to have been given was not adduci;d, The police, instead of try- ing to trace the pistol, used all their I ffortg trying to prove acts of hornorality against the Prisoner. The evidence proved that the prisoner lived on good term': with his wife. The Hill against Noel was afte'rWar& thrown out hy the grand jury.

div.head: TALE OF LOITEMOOR.
div.p: A TALE OF LOITEMOOR.
CIIAPTER XLVIL
HER ANSWER.

That message was more than startling—it. was appalling. In her wildest imaginings, in'her search through the whole range of possibilities, Miss Norreys had notlully dared to imagine any possibility like this. It smote her like an awful blow.

She reeled against the wall, looking as if struck with death. The telegram was crushed in her hand, and clenched in a grip of steel. She looked as if she .were about to faint or die, Then she rallied suddenly by a stiperhumian effort, and tettered back to her meat, her face like ashes, her eyes :wild and ,string, her white lips moving ,fcehly, but giving emission to no sound.
Her aspczt chilled the nuu;quie with an awful terror.

"What is it?" be exclaimed. "Have you ill news, MissA orreys . Size waved him from her, shrinking back as if his vvry touch were pollution. There was terror of him in that look—frightful unmistakeable horror. Had she gone mad under some fearful shock?

"Shall I call some one ?" he exclaimed, vrild with earth. "You are ill." With a supreme effort of her will she commanded the emotions that raged in her heart like furious beasts of pity. - • . "No—no! she gasped. "I want no one. Leave no to myself. • I would he alone." - The marquis, without a word, obeyed her. He saw that she was suffering intensely, and although consumed with curiosity and jealousy, he yet sub- mitted wisely to her command. "1 witi stand guard at the end, of the avenue," he said, res.pectfully and very quietly, quite as if .such scenes were of every day oceurrenge in his ex- perience, and not at all remarkable. "No one shall intrude upon you. I will hear when you call me."

He moved away as one moves in a sick chamber, softly; almost noiselessly. Miss Norreys looked after him with that stare of horror seeming frozen in her eyes, and slowly mingling in it an expression of bitterest hatred and loathing. Marry him !" the thought struggled through all the chaos of her mind tierce and strong. "I would rather die.

• She shivered as with an ague. ' . He walked to the end of the avenue, and stood there under an orange tree in a careless attitude, guarding her solitude. And she—left aloneamid the odorous blooms and goluen iruits ana mellow tights—opened the paper again and read those strange words, every syllable of which burnt its way into her brain. And then she gave way to a paroxysm of emotion, all the greater for her recent stern self-repression. Her lips quivered, her brown eyes flooded with tears, and she raised the paper to her lips and kissed it passionately again and again. Then, as if loathing herself for the aetionohe looked upon the paper in disgust, and deliberately tore it in pieces so minute that Lord Darkwood would have tried in vain to decipher a word .of its contents.
"Not dead !" she whispered. ".Not dead 1"

The words sounded strangely to her ears. "Not drowned !" she muttered. "He came back to England six months ago! He came to England—where he should have been safe and secure—be came to England!" she repeated, with ticreasing emphasis. `• What does that mean?" Ah, she hardly dared acknowledged even to her.; self.

"Six months ago Captain Tollish was safely established at Dunholm Castle as Lord Darkwood, she thought. "Did the real Lord Darkwood re- turn to Dititholin Castle? If he did—as seems probable—what then?" The question was one bristling with importance. She turned it over and over in her own mind. And gradually there grew within her into vast propor- tions that horror of suspicion against the present Lord Darkwood that she had felt in the moment she had sent him from her. Had he seen his cousin in the hour of the latter's return.

Upon that final question everything was hinged. "I must know—l must know!" she thought, in a very frenzy. "Where would he be during six months? Perhaps he had died in England? There is some mystery in the case which I must fathom. The man who stands ',ender may be guiltless of bloodshed. I think he would scarcely dare kill his rival—and yet there was so much at stake! But Lord Dark wood could not have reappeared at Dun- holm Castle secretly and unrecognised. He probably had -a relapse of illness in Loudon, was unable to make known his identity, old died unknown. Bad as he is, I can't think that Captain Tollish would be guilty of deliberate murder—or that he had an opportunity to commit it." She sat there among theblooms and glossy leaves a long time thinking over these thoughts, and others like these. And gradually she grew calm. The lovely face hardened in every feature and grew strong and resolute. " I hate them both with a bitter unrelenting hatred !" she said to herself. "So that his blood stains not his rival's hand, I do not care that he is dead ! His death wipes out the past, so far as he is concerned. It remains for me to deal, with the living. I think I will marry Lord Darkwood." She looked towards him with an uncontrollable loathing. He seemed to feel her glance and turned around. She lifted up one gloved hand and beckoned ,to him.

He obeyed with alacrity. The storm had passed and no traces were left, save in the languor of her movements and the pallor that still dwelt in her complexion. She was gracious in her manner, with a reserve, however, which had not marked it before, and which piqued him.

"You are better" he exclaimed, eagerly. "I am well, thanks," she apswered. "My tele- gran: contained news that disturbed me deeply: that is all." She dismissed the Subject with the scraps of paper she flung frown her dress, and he could not return to it.

"Our conversation suffered a little interruption my lord," she said, gently. "I fear you will think the interruption a rude one. Let us return to what you were saying." "'With all my heart," he replied, trembling,' anticipating his dismissal. "I asked you to be my wife, Miss Norreys. I love you, and if you will trust your happiness to my keeping, I will endea- vour to be worthy of the trust.' "I will not refuse you, my lord," said the lady, with a gracious sweetness that took the sting from her words. ." lam sensible of the honour you do me, but if I do not refuse you, neither can I accept you. Give me a week for consideration. At the end of that period I will give you my answer. And that answer will be, she added, deliberately, "if nothing occurs to change my mind, an affirma- tive."

The gri;at dome of glass, the flowers and lights, seemed to swim around Lord Darkwood in a great chaos. An immense exultatinu filled his being to its utmost capacity, He believed that his prize was won. He caujght up her hand and kissed it in a transport of delight. ' "You are all coming to-Morrow to the castle," he exelairried. "If I knight only present you as its fu,ture mistress !" _

" Give me a week 1" insisted Miss Norreys, grow- ing colder. "And during that timo do not speak to me of love or marriage." It was so settled, and presently the hostess was conducted back to the ball-room by her suitor, who seemed to walk on air. He was in the seventh heaven of delight. He considered himself her accepted suitor. But, although she intended to marry him, although her scheme of revenge seemed so near its fulfilment, her heart lay like lead in her bosom. She would have her revenge; but, like Samson's, it would involve her own destruction.
CHAPTER xLvirt. A GLIMPSE OF HER LOVER.

The spectre of Dunholin Castle ruins had not been quiescent during the past few months. Not that he had been seen—there was no one adven- turous enough in the household to risk an encounter with him. But the servants whispered to each other of spectral lights at the hour of midnight in the ruins, and one or two asseverated that they had seen an awful figure, with streaming hair and bloody visage, flitting before the ruined windows, and surrounded by a lurid glare of light. These stories had been repeated to the Lady Georgina by her maid. Lord Darkwoocl's heiress, with big round eyes and pallid complexion, re- peated the tale to her governess-companion. Gwen laughed them to scorn, declaring their author to be endowed with a vivid imagination and unlimited superstition. Yet none knew better than Gwen that these wild stories had a certain foundation in fact.
Ber roomsl situated over the great bancenting

hall of the castle, were upon the -opposite hide oT the quadrangle to the main portion of the ruins. And night after night she had seen a light flitting palely through the ruins, but she had never seen the figure of anyone, human or spectre—nothing but the feeble, glimmering light. It appeared sometimes at midnight, sometimes later. Some nights it did not appear at all. Gwen was inclined to be wakeful, and she often watched for the mysterious gleam, wondering at it, and constructing in her own mind fanciful explanations of its origin.

But when the servants began to whisper about it in the servants' hall, and to recall the ancient tragedy of centuries since, and shudder over it, and grow frightened, the nightly gleams died out, and the spectral lights were seen no more. It was the morning after the ball at Beeehmont, and the morning of the' day appointedior the, visit to Dunholm Castle of Miss Norreys and her guests. • Lord DarkwOod, regaraing himself as the ac- cepted suitor of the lady of Deeehmont, and desir- ing to show himself and hfs possessions to their best advantage in her sight, paid personal attention to the. preparations for he reception and entertain- ment of his expected visitors. • . _ _

He had consulted his cook, a Frenchman of the true cordon bleu, in regard to the menu of the dinner to be served upon the great occasion. • He had given minute instructions to his daughter in regard to her toilet and deportment, for he had decided that the Lady Georgina was to make her appearance; and he.had visited. the ruins and per- sonally superintended their preparation for the dance to be held M them by moonlight.. . The day dawned clear and bright and pleasant. Lord Darkwood had not returned home from the Beechmont ball until nearly dawn, and he slept until noon. When he awoke, Pietro was not in attendance upon him, and he was obliged to submit to the ministrations of his second valet, a stupid, good-natured fellow, who was in reality the ser- vant of the Maltese, and more in awe of him than of his master. • The under valet gossiped as he dressed his lordship, and repeated the tales current in the servants' hall concerning the spectre. The marquis listened with a brow dark as a thundercloud, and he exclaimed harshly against such folly, desiring a stop to be put to such ridicu- lous stories. He descended to breakfast moodily, and afterwards retired to the library. Here he rang his bell, and ordered Pietro to be sent to him. The Maltese, sleek and silent as usual, dressed entirely in black, appeared at. his summons. "It seems to me that you are missing all the morning," observed the marquis angrily. "Why were you absent from your usual duties!" • "I was in the old banqueting hall in the ruins, _ signor," replied the valet, smoothly. "The sot.- vants are waxing the floor for the dance, and com- pleting their preparations for the evening. I hut just looked in. When I returned, you were at breakfast."

• Lord Darkwood turned abruptly, facing the Maltese abruptly. "What's this nonsense the servants are gabbling, Pietro," he demanded, "about the Darkwood ghost?" "Oh, you have heard that story, signor?" in. quired Pietro, carelessly. "I heard it weeks ago." "What does it mean ? "

"It all sprung from certain visits I made to the ruins after midnight months ago," declared Pietro, steadily. "The light I carried—it was that old lantern—chanced to be seen by some wakeful servant, and the story has been repeated until it has grown into a great tale of a bloody spectre, with a red light enveloping him." "And you hav'n't been in the dungeons for some time V' "
"Not until last evening, when I obeyed your command, and went below to see that all was safe." "It was safe?"

"Perfectly. Yet, signor, I should advise you not to permit these visitors to go below," said Pietro, in a low voice. "You see, my lord, if an owl but hoots below there, as he did when the young ladies went through the dungeons, some line lady will shriek that it is a ghost, and the party may wish to investigate—" "I will lock up the dungeons and conceal the keys," interrupted Lord Du.rkwood, hastily. "When my daughter and her governess visited the dungeons and heard that owl, and thought it the cry of a ghost, I was in mortal terror. For the —the body lay then upon one of the dungeon floors, did it not ?"

"Stark and stiff as on the night when you and I, Signor, carried it down there. We had not had time and inclination to bury it, you remember." "Yes, I remember. I ánf not a coward; and nub superstitious," said the marquis, with a shiver, "but I could not look again upon that dead face, nor could I help,to bury him. But you attended to it—he is buried?"

"Out of sight, under six feet of dirt," declared the Maltese. "The body lay on the rock floor for months, mouldering. But when you told me it must be got out of the way, and offered me a hun- dred pounds to bury it, I took the matter in hand. You remember when we went down together into the ruins, to settle what was to be done, and met the strange couple coming out of the doorway. Well, after that I was occupied several nights in the task, and it was my light the servants saw and took for that of a spectre. I worked a dozen nights, more or less, in all," said Pietro, glibly. "It was a horrible task, signor, and I think my pay for it should have been dhubled." "It shall be," declared his master. "I could not bury the body out of doors," re- marked the Maltese. "I dared not dig a hole in the gardens or park, or elsewhere, the gardeners and labourers are so prying and 'busy. I could not fling it in the pond or in Dark River, for it would have been found immediately. The floors of most of the dungeons are of solid rock, and of course could not avail me in my work. But in the far tower in the black dungeons I found a hard clay soil, which I picked up. And it was there," and the valet lowered his voice to a whisper, "that I buried him."

"Rave you levelled the grave ?" "Yes, signor, sod I carried most of the dirt away in bags," said Pietro. "I knew not where to put it, and I feared its nature, so different from the surface soil, would betray it. So I rowed out in the pond and flung it into the water." "A wise precaution. But some dirt still re- mains ?"

"A heap of it on the floor. I have not had time to remove it, signor. I will do so as soon as pos- sible. If you• had helped it might have been ddne by this." "I would not help—l would not do that work " cried Lord Darkwood quickly—i" not for a for- tune."

"I am made of tougher stuff," said Pietro, smil- ing. "We Maltese are more used to bloodshed than you cold Englishmen. But even I would not go through this digging and anxiety a'nd hard work again—not for a thousand pounds.' "you shall not be stinted in your reward," said the marquis. " But if there is fresh dirt still on that grave in the dungeon, no one must go below. Some inquisitive person might pull ruin down upon our heads. Lock up the dungeons. Keep the keys, Pietro. And when you can, finish your work below, stamp down the grave, and make all secure." •

The Maltese assented, and presently retired. Then the marquis leaned back in his chair and drew a great sigh of relief. He had often thought during the last month of that ghastly object lying on the dark dungeon floor, of the white face and fair hair hidden amid the blackness of gloom, and determined to muster up courage to assist in burying it for ever from all possibility of human search, but he had never been able to look upon his victim again. The Maltese was more used to such frightful ex- periences, and he had confided the task to him.

" Pietro does not look upon murder as we Eng- lish do," he muttered. "He thinks all the better of me for having rid myself of my rival and enemy. I am fortunate in having attached to me a man of his,charactereand turn of mind." He smiled s'omplacently, flinging off the load of care and anxiety that had rested so heavily upon him.

"Now for enjoyment,".be soliloquised. "Now for unalloyed happiness! No obstacle can come between me and my beautiful Sicily. She intends to marry me, and I shall urge a speedy marriage. I am impatient to call her mine." . . . . .
As the hour approached for the arrival of his guests' he made a careful toilet, and took his place in • the drawing-room.
_ The Lady Georgina, in a dress of pale blue silk, with embroidered Swiss overdress, presently joined him. •

Ws. Dover, in a long dress of lavender silk, with a coiffure of black and white lace, also appeared. It was Lord Darkwood's wish that his lady housez' keeper should matronisc his daughter. Gwen" was not asked to appear in the drawing. room. The Lady cieorgina was divided between affectionlor her beautiful companion and jealousy of her.. She would not consent that Gwen should join the company upon this occasion, and the young girl remained. therefore, in her own rooms. Lord

Darkwood not desiring tb contest the point with his daughter. As an exploration of the castle was the project in hand, the carriages from Beechmont began to arrive about four o'clock.. Miss Norreys came last of all in a waggonette with LOrd Chilton. The guests were all radiant in fresh toilets, alicl were all in Sue spirits, notwithstanding the previous night's ball at Beeehmont. Miss Norreys wore a black sille dress, embroidered with pink rosebuds. Her corsage was cut in pent' padour fashion, with a square neck, and sleeves cut off at the elbow, and frilled with lace. She ("reeted her host with a rising flush on her Pale olive t Zheeks, but her manner was devoid of consciousness. She was gracious, yet cold as an iceberg. ,He felt his love for her glow and kindle within him, and be longed to prodaim to those around him that this superb woman had half promised to become bis wife. Miss Norreyswas very courteous to the LOY Georgina and to Mrs. Dover. Then her glances sought for missing_Gwen. , In the press of her • many recent duties, and the excitement attendant upon the projects she had in hand, she had tleg• lected to visit Gwen as she had intended, but she had thought of her many times. The girl's beauty and ihnocence, sweetness And loveliness, had touched her heart. She had grown to love her with an intensity that surprised her- self; for she was not one to love readily. She haci even thought of a plan by which she might rem_ ,_eve Gwen to her own house and protection, but saw being difficult was in abeyance. "Is not Miss Myner able to join us, Lady Geer- giar," she asked, perceptibly disappointed. • No," answered Lord blarkwood's daughter, falsely. "Her arm still pains her. She litgged be excused excused from seeing anyone to-day. The excite. meat is not good for her." "Would she not see me?" asked Miss Is.TorreYe' "Might.l not go up to her room ?" " Impossible !" said Lady Georgina. "Site unable to see anyone, Miss Norreys. But I wt tell her of your kind inquiries after her." The East India heiress was not quite satisfiet but she was compelled to appear so. She leoge„ to see Gwen, and her failure to do so was a seYerei disappointment than she would have devwe possible. The visitors explored the gardens and conserva- tories, the park, and the various objects of outdoor interest. They rowed in barges on Dark and returned to the castle between .five emu o'clock, eager to examine the 'ruins. div.head: ROMANCE OF LIFE.
div.p: ROMANCE OF LIFE.

. . The story of Enoch Arden is a very comMOTI one. Husbands are continually turning up at inconvenient times, when they ought, as they are supposed to be, in another sphere. The whole story of lost heirs and defunct claimants show that people who are supposed to be dead and buried unexpectedly appear upon the scene. But when a man has been attended by doctors and subjected to every treatinent,and has been told that his case is hopeless, coming from such sources, it is generally accepted as the inevitable. However, experience proves conclusively that many have been saved from the grave, despite such gloomy Prognoses. Mr.Wm.Bailey,late Quartermaster-Sergeant, Royal Horse Artillery, 30, Beecholme-road, Clapton, ~ondsn, writes : "Six years ago, while in service in India, I was attacked with terrible pains in my chest, Shortness of breath,general enervation,and giddiness. My eyesight rapidly failed, and my feet and legs commenced to swell. The swelling increased,extending to my body. was full of water, my feet, legs, body, face, and even flay eyes,were swollen to a frightful size. I lay in bed a elpless mass. I was advised to try Warner's Safe Cure. 1 did so. lam cured, and Warner's Safe Cure did it. _Comrades all ; my coffin was ordered, but thanks to warner% Safe Cure, the order his not been executed."

div.p: RECEPTION TO THE REV. JOSEPH ELLISON.

There was a very pleasant gathering of Latchford Baptists and temperance workers, at the Temper- ance flail, on Monday evening. Its object was to extend a welcome to the Rev. Joseph Ellison, and Mrs. Ellison, upon their return from America to Latchford for a vacation. There were present. Particularly many members of the local order of Good Tempfara, of which body Mr. Ellison was an exceedingly ardent and enthusiastic worker. The chair ought to have been taken by Mr. H. H. Drury, D.C.T. of t.-'t ockport,but in his ,unavoidable absence, his place was taken by Mr. Thomas Anderson, D.Co. Ile on behalf of the District Executive of Good Templars, presented an address to the Rev. Joseph Ellison, and also offered him a warm welcome, be- sides many words of encouragenient and congratu- lation. The address was signed by the following: —H. H. Drury. T. Anderson, D. Fogg, J. C. Brand- rith ,111. E. Armstrong. T.Underwood,T.Ellison,A.Dew, B. Bauman, and J. Edwards. Mr. Thomas Underwood, of Hyde, addressed the meeting, and in the course of his remarks said they, as the Executive, thought the present was an opportueity of showing the respect they entertained towards Mr. Ellison's parents, by recogniz- ing his presence in England. They could not forget that Mr. and Mrs. Ellison were natives of Latchford and had worked for God and the temperance movement. Mr. Ellison was well-known in Latchford from a boy for his earnest desire to lead a sober and godly life. They knew that the example set him by his parents was a good one, and that Ile appreciated the home training he received. He was a young man who had devoted his life to do what little he could for the " betterment " of his fellow-creatures, and one result of it was that -they as temperance people that night wished to send him back lighter-hearted to America, and to let him, along with his wife, feel that his efforts for the redemption of the country from the evil of drink were highly appre- ciated. When Mr. Ellison left this country for America, he had no intention of occupying the position he now held, but he had gained it by his sheer, hard, stedfast labours for Christ. He was sure there was not one of them that would not feel delighted at his having at- tained it. (Applause.) Latchford owed a great deal to the Ellison family, and they thought the present would be a timing opportunity to honour the father and the mother by presenting the address that they had done. When Mr. Ellison knew that it was given in that sense, no doubt he would honour it all the more. (Applause.) The Rev. J. W. Varley, flaptist minister, as a per- sonal friend of the Rev. Joseph Ellison, delivered a characteristic speech, brimming over with the sparkling fun with which the rev, gentleman enlivens social gatherings with which he is connected,and at the same time paying an earnest and sincere tribute to the value of his reverend friend. lie said he came there that night because he was in deep and complete sympathy with Mr. Ellison, having known him for many years, and having been associated with him in many ways in Christian service. He could speak of Mr. Ellison as a personal friend, and the first thing that he admired in him was, that in his (Mr. Varley's) judgment he was a consecrated roan. One reason why he welcomed Mr. , Ellison was l-ecatise he could see in him something of the image of his Divine Lord and Master. That, t him, was the chief thing in a man's character, and if a man had not that, his life was doomed to utter failure. From his contact with Mr. Ellison and from the gracious letters that he had had from him he knew that lie had Christ in his heart. (Applause.) In the young lady he had recently married, Mr. Ellison had a wife, whom he knew, from personal acquaintance, would be truly a comforter and helpmeet to him. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Wilkinson said he welcomed Mr. Ellison as one who had laboured together with him in Sunday School and Church work, and also some little in temperance work. He had always foind him one whose heart was in the right place, and he hoped Olathe and Mrs. Ellison would have long and happy lives. (Applause.)—Mr. Drew, district chaplain, and the Chairman having spoken, the Rev. Joseph Ellison responded. He naturally did so in a very feeling way, and re- counted the many local associations and friends, many of whom were pregent, to whom he attributed much of his enthusiasm to serve God, and especially to work in the temperance cause. During the years in which he had laboured It Latchford, and during his labours in America, he never lost sight of one thing, the life of Christ, a life which he did his bet to make his pattern, and to adhere to with an unswerving con- stancy which he knew was a gift from his father, for they knew aS well as he, what a trait that was in his parent's character. He afterwards spoke vigorously in the cause of temperance.—Mr. Harrison, who had been a personal friend of Mr. Ellison, next spoke a few hearty words of welcome,and in the course of a pleasant little speech, he confessed his weakness to overcome his friend's clerical title. He said he couldn't seem to•fall into the way of calling him " the Rev. Mr. Joseph Ellison," now. He had tried it,but he didn't know why it was, he'd have to give it up and simply call him Joe, as of yore.—(Laughter.). The meeting formed itself into a social gathering, when personal welcomes were ex- tended to Mr. and Mrs. Ellison, the latter of whom, to the delight of her lady friends, appeared in her bridal costume.

div.head: GROSS NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON. A MISERABLE HOME.
div.p: GROSS NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON. A MISERABLE HOME.

- - Before the Warrington magistrates on Monday, John Dillon and Sarah Dillon, residing at 18, Ship- yard, were each charged with neglecting to keep heir children in nourishment and in a proper con- dition, on the 2nd inst.—Mr. J. D. Buekton prose- cuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C.—Mr. Buckton in opening the case said that the prisoners were prosecuted for neglecting three children, Theresa aged five years, Ellen aged three years and May aged seven months. The two elder children were neglected chiefly by want of proper clothing, and being in a filthy condition, but the youngest was also short of nourishment. It seemed to be caused by drink. When the children were first seen, the male prisoner came in drunk,and drinking seemed to be going on wholesale. He was an army pensioner and a large portion of the inhabitants of Ship-yard were' disposing of the pension money. When Inspector Uphill, N.S.P.C.C., went into the house he found the house in a I very filthy condition insomuch that Dr. Peacocke who was called in gave a certificate of admission for tne younger child into the workhouse hospital. The prisoners had ample means, as the man gets 245. per week as a labourer on the Ship Canal and also a pension which amounts to 2s. per week. Inspector Uphill said that from information he received lie went to the house of the prisoners on the Ist Inst., in company with P.C. Corbett. There was no one in the house at first, but soon after the female prisoner came in with the youngest child in her arms. It was sucking from a bottle with a 'stinking "tube attached. In the bottle was some water with a little bread. The body was in a filthy condition and much emaciated and excreta had dried upon it. The mother showed a soap box as being used for a cradle in which there was a lot of dirty rags. The only food in the house was a loaf of bread. Witness went upstairs and saw Theresa and Nellie , lying upon a mattress which WAS almost rotten and flies were almost devouring them. There was an old bin out of which excreta was flowing about the room, and the stench was almost unbearable. Witness went and brought in Dr. Peacocke and whets they returned they found the male prisoner in the house very drunk. Dr. Peacocke, on examining the child, immediately gave an order for its removal to the Workhouse hospital. The child only weighed 8 lbs. 4 czs., on its admission to the Workhouse and in a week it increased one Ih., one oz. The normal weight of a child of its age was 13 lbs. 4 oz. when questioned the mother said that she got a half- pennyworth of milk per day for the child. It had n•t had any food from three o'clock on the day previous to a quarter to one on Sunday afternoon. Dr. Peacocke said that he WAS called in by the last witness to examine the child. He found it in an exteed- ingly filthy and emaciated condition. He had examined the contents of the bottle out of which the child was feeding and f Rind it to be water with bread, which was decomposing and sour, and quite sufficient to kill it. The child was not suffering from any disease but from neglect. He corroborated the Inspector's statement as to the condition of the rooms above. C. Corbett also corroborated Inspector Uphill's statement. Amelia Longley, workhouse nurse, said 'that when athnitted to the workhouse the child ate food raven- ously. The male prisoner called on his behalf Mrs. Speakman who said that she supplied them with milk three times a day, and Mr. Glynn who said that they had , sufficient nrovisions and that he did not know the children to be neglected. Inspector Bowen said that when he saw the children on Saturday they were very clean, but he had not seen , them Previously. During the whole of the hearing of the case the male prisoner caused much amusement by his questionings and statements and also by his manner. Before the bench gave their decision Alderman Wright wished to know how the Inspector ant his information about the cases to which Inspector Uphill replied that lie waainformed by the police. Dr. Gornall said tliat he could give him a great many of these cases if he wanted them. Alderman Harrison in givinn, the decision of the bench said that the case was one of gross nerlect. He was surprised to see that such a decent-looking woman as the female prisoner hail caused such injury to her offspring. The magistrates w'ould send the husband to gaol for a month and the female prisoner to 14. days' imprisonment.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 15, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 15, 1893.
A WARRINGTON MIRACLE.
A COOK'S EXTRAORDINARY NARRATIVE.

On the occasion of a recent fête in Warrington, any- one's attention would have been attracted, as was ours, to a young woman of about 30 years, who stood near Arpley Station, at a spot where the crowd was thinnest. Although pale, her face wore a contented smile—a pecu- liar smile of happiness, quiet, yet net sad, but just tinged with something like thoughtfulness that showed the woman knew what trouble and pain were—not from ' present suffering, but from past experience. That was the first " Walking "Day she had seen for six years ! six long weary years, during which she lay almost un- able to move; given up by medical men as one hopelessly incurable from the terrible afflictions which she had contracted like many another woman now-a-days, through unswerving devotion to work. It was fairly well known amongst a large circle of people that only during the past month had she been able to walk three. yards, without help. „ Consequently, as day by day she began to walk slowly about without assistance, undertaking longer journeys each day, the people about Heaton-street, off John-street, where Miss Margaret Ann Bradshaw lives, opened their eyes wider with surprise and said to her : " Why ! What have you been doing ? It's like a miracle to see you walking about." " Well " Miss Bradshaw would reply " It is a miracle —thine through Dr.Williarns' Pink Pills for Pale People." " Dr. Williams' Pink Pills ? What are they ?"

" They are manufactured by Dr. William's Medicine Company. They have worked a miracle in this case." This an Examiner reporter was told, as Miss Bradshaw was pointed out to him on Walking Day,then a good half mile from home, a distance she had covered in company with her sister. . .

A'day or two after the reporter set out to 23, Ileatn- street to inquire into the facts of this startling story. He was received by the sick woman's sister, who ex- pressed her pleasure at seeing anyone who had come to talk about her sister's recoverV. Just then the invalid walked with a steady gait, and cheerful look from an adjoining room, to where he sat. Is this remarkable story of your re;overy true, Miss Bradshaw," said the reporter. _ _

"Yes, indeed it is ! And I'm pleased whenever I can tell anyone about it." " What were you suffering from ? " " The doctors said it was paralysis of the spine, and rheumatisM of the nerves." " When did you first commence to suffer."

"Six years ago. Up to then I was very strong and healthy, and was in the habit of working hard. For more than five years I was a cook at an eating house in town,anal during the whole of that time I was con- stantly employed between three ovens, and three fires. It was the effect of that upon my nerves and spine, that brought the illness on chiefly ; so the doctors say. But I did not feel it then. It was not until I loft and took up other work of s different kind, that the trouble com- tnonced. I was ne longer engaged in a hot reeking room, and now every limb in my body seemed to get cold and chilled, even in warm weather. The doctor told me afterwards that it was a reaction setting in. This had been going on for some time, when one day all my strength seemed to suddenly leave me, and I fell to the ground. Oh! It was the commencement of a bitter time for me. It was the first ot those strokes with which I have been afflicted. I was put to bed, and was unable to stand or move my limbs for a long time. It took three persons to dress me and carry me to a chair where I was pronped up. This continued for twelve months, and then I had 'another stroke. My doctor then said he would recommend me to induce my friends to procure admittance for me into a lespital at Manchester I for incurable invalids. But I refused to go." " And we're not sorry you did, now," said her sister.

_ The invalid continued her story. A little more than 12 months after the second stroke she had a third, and the doctors despaired of her life. Her relatives began to seek other advice and other remedies, but nothing ever seemed to give her even temporary strength. So she continued, as she and every one else believed, a con- firmed cripple and invalid. When feeling at her best,it was an exhausting task for her to move from one room 'to another, with the assistance of her sister. "Well, some weeks ago," she continued. "My sister Fanny came home and said she had been reading in one of the papers of a case similar to my own having been cured by Dr.Willianis' Pink Pills for Pale People. They suggested that I should try them. I censented, not that I had any faith in them,for I had lost every faith in medicine. By this time I was suffering from several other ailments. I began to suffer from deafness, which commenced with jingling noises in the ears; and then my eyesight became affected. My hands and fingers were stiff—as stiff and as lifeless as wood. Well, the first thing I noticed, after I had taken half a box of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, was that I could just mote my fingers about, without bend- ing the joints. An entire change came over my disposi- tion ; the nasty sensations in the head almost vanished, and my eyesight became ;well again -and for the first time for years life began to appear bright. By the time I had finished the first tox of Pills; I could absolutely peel potatoes, so you may imagine the effect there had been upon my hands. I could feel the benefits of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills then,and I took them regularly until, now—l have had four boxes, and I can scarcely believe myself the wonderful change that has taken ;place in me. As you see I can now walk almost with perfect ease—and certainly without any assistance." And Miss Bradshaw rose here, and walked round the room with nothing but a scarcely noticeable stiffness in her gait. ""
" Ynu are sure it is the Pills that are curing you ?"

_ "Certainly," said Miss Bradshaw, with a smile. "There is not a shadow of a doubt about it. I take the pills regularly, and although it is said they cure gradu- ally, I could never have believed there was any remedy so speedy in its effect." "We only wish we had heard of Dr. Wiliams Com- pany's Pink Pills before," said the invalid's sister. I suffer from nervousness and indigestion, and since my sister has been taking the pills I have tried them, and been completely free both from nervousness and indi- gestion. But we can ali assure you of the miraculous effect they have had upon my sister."

_ Miss Bradshaw's statement has been borne out in de- 11 tail by both her sisters, many of her neighbours,and her brother, Mr. Robert Brw:esliaw, also of 23, lleaton-street. ' Indeed, the story of this " miracle" has become so well known that quite a demand is being made by other suf- ferers for rink Pills, in consequence of which Mr. J. I Rymer Young, chemist, of Sankey-st.,ha4 commeaced to sell the pills. One of Miss Bradshaw's neighbours, Mrs. Louisa Wildgoose, of No. 7, Heaton-street, told the re- porter :—" I was so surprised at the great change 'in Miss Bradshaw, that I asked her what remedy she had discovered. She told me she was using Dr. William's Pink Pills for Pale People, My husband had seen accoants of marvellous cures by these pills in the papers, so he persuaded me to get a box, which I did, from Mr. Young, of Sankey-street. This was three weeks ago. Eleven weeks ago I had a stroke and felt the effect in my shoulder and arm until I had taken three pills ; then the pain and stiffness disappeared. I also suffered from dizziness in the head, but that has disappeared since I have been taking the pills. But I vas surprised at the wonderful effect the pills had upon Miss Bradshaw. I believe several people have since commenced to take them for strokes."
