Mr. Deakin, the silvery tones of Mr. Kniveton, and the burning address of Mr. Blagg had dealt with everything so thoroughly. Mr. Blegg seemed to think that if they had been more considerate to the Tories they would have managed to have got the flonie Rule Bill through in this session. The Tory members of the House of Commons were very like everyone else when they were outside, they appeared very kindly disposed, but the moment they got on the benches they seemed to be absolutely transformed. No amount of conciliation from Mr. Gladstone, who had shown them every consideration, night after night for many weary weeks, would have persuaded the Tories to pass the Bill this session. To his mind they gave them rope enough—(laughter)—and they had used it in the old satisfactory proverbial fashion. (Laughter.) It was absolutely necessary that all the Bills and measures of this character should be well considered by the House of Commons. This Bill had been discusser Lad nauseum every line had been discussed, morning, noon and night, in season and out of season, and with reason and without reason. (Laughter.) Everyone of the clauses had been discussed over and over again, and there had not been any unjust and unfair treatment of the 'lory party in Parliament.--e Mr. Blagg : I have net been complaining for the Tories.—Mr. Brunner continued: Mr. Illagg, Mr. Deakin, and Mr. Kniveton had said it was absolutely necessary that this Bill, which was , of far-reaching importance, should be well and fully discussed. He said it again, that the Bill had from the beginning not only been well discussed, not only fully discussed, not only fairly dis- cussed, but it had been most unfairly discussed, and he wanted them t..) assure their friends and politi- cal enemies there had been absolutely no foundation for the accusation that the Liberal party had unfairly stopped this discussion. •He was satisfied that he should go back to London cheered with their hearty sup. pert and help to carry through the 13111 to a successful issue. (Applause.) Now they were occasionally brought into contact on both sides with the leaders of the parties, and he had been honoured with more than one interview with members of the Cabinet. Not having at that time the fear of Mr. Blagg's reproof upon his mind, he assured every member of the Government and especi- ally of the Cabinet, that in the application of the patent Tory machinery, that the Liberal Constituency of North- wich would support them. (Applause.) He had the honour of being appointed to represent a large com- mittee of Radical members of the House of Commons, and at the end of the interview they had with Mr. Fowler, the President of the Local Government Board, he ventured to express an opinion and join in the opinion of his friends that alter the Home Rule Bill the Local Government (England and Wales )Bill should come next. (Applause.) There had never been in his opinion pre- sented to Parliament a Bill so thoroughly and purely de mocratic as the Local Government Bill. He knew of no Bill which would have so powerful an influence in rais- ing the self respect of the men who lived in their vil- lages than this Parish District Councils Bill. It would have the effect of interesting in local affairs, men and women who lived in the small towns and villages ; it would have the effect Gf inducing them to take for the first time a keen and intelligent interest in their local affairs. It would put every man living in the village on a level with the squire in political affairs. He was thoroughly convinced it would have the effect of making them more comfortable as regarded their materiai wants. He was sure if they had the Bill passed into law it would very greatly diminish poverty and would enhance the material well being of the people of this country. He was not only enthusiastically democratic, but he was also a man of business, and he must say this was not a Bill that did much in the direction of economy. In 1871, Mr. Goschen said 6s. 8.1. of every pound expended for local government was wasted money and he hoped his constituents would back him (Mr. Brunner) if, in spite of the remonstrances from the Gov- ernment, he ventured to set down on paper and to pro- pose with some degree of persistency such amendments as he considered would make the Bill a measure of economy, as well as the measure having the merits he had ascribed to it. (Applause.) He was not one of those who last Thursday night voted against the sixth clause of the Home Rule Bill. That clause provided fora second chamber of men elected by a restricted franchise; it was a vast improvement on the House of Lords, although perhaps it did not carry democratic principles far enough, but he would not throw an improvement away because it was not as good as it ought to be. (Hear, hear.) If he were tempted to vote with the Irish when they were voting against the Government, never would he vote against the Government when the Irish were voting for them. (Applause ) They had sent him to Parliament first and foremost to vote against the Tories. (Laughter and applause.) He thanked them for passing the resolution,which would strengthen him for the work he would resume on his return to London. (Loud applause.) Mr. Mclntyre moved and Mr. Bennett seconded that a hearty vote of thanks be accorded to the Chairman. me motion was carried unanimously and the meeting terminated.

div.head: NOB.TIEWICH DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. , __- ANNUAL MEETING AT NORTHWICH. SPEECH BY MR. BRUNFER, M.P.
div.p: NOB.TIEWICH DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. , __- ANNUAL MEETING AT NORTHWICH. SPEECH BY MR. BRUNFER, M.P.

The annual meeting of the Council of the North- wich Division Liberal Association was held at the Gladstone Club, Northwich, on Saturday afternoon. There was a large attendance of members, every part of the division being represented. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., was present. In the absence of Mr. H. Brett, Mr. A. Fletcher presided.

TEE SECRETARY'S REPORT. The Secretary (Mr. William Handley) read his annual report, in which lie stated that several circumstances had combined to delay their annual meeting to a much later period than usual, but this had in no way inter- fered with the prosecution of the ordinary work of the association, and the greater interval of time afforded a broader view of the work and aims of the Liberal party since its return to power, and an opportunity of arriving at a truer estimate of the spirit which animated the party, whose beast it was that they were the saviours of the constitution. At their last annual meeting their special work was the adoption for the fourth time of Mr. Brunner as the Parliamentary embodiment of the robust Liberalism of the Northwich Division' and as they had somewhere read " Wisdom is justified of her children," the wisdom of their choice was more than justified by , the spirit of enthusiasm with which Mr. Brunner was again received throughout the whole constituency, the earnest work evoked to secure his return, and which was equally characteristic of every polling district in the division, and the increased majority accorded him on the day of election, a majority the more remarkable as it was conceded by all that never In previous elections, had the Liberal party been confronted by such a com- pact, united, and determined force. It might be re- membered that the last annualreport in view of the then coining conflict pointed out that even to retain the per- centage of majority as compared with the election of 1887, it would need to be increased from 1,129 to 1,217, but at ths close of the poll on July 18th, 1892, this anti- cipated number had been exceeded, and stood proudly at 1,255. Many were the reasons, or excuses, advanced by their opponents for that, to them, astounding result, but the most remarkable explanation was that given ut- terance to by their Chairman, after more than six months' fly fishing in the sea of dire extremity in the hope of presenting a digestible morsel for their consolation. " The contest resulted in a majority of 1,255 votes, which practically meant that if 628 persons had voted differently, Mr. Brunner would not have been returned. From what he (the chairman) had seen and heard since, he believed that Mr.Brunner's return was mainly due to the large amount of influence Mr. Brunner had over his employee. They had all heard what had been the result of the Meath petitions, and they had heard of a good deal of clercial intimida- tion, but be had very little doubt that in the Northwich Division were certainly 628 men, who at heart were Con- servative, but who from the position they occupied either abstained from voting or did not vote according to the dictates of their consciences. He did not blame them,for after all, a man's bread and butter was his first consider- ation, but if a petition had been put forth the result might have been very similar to that at Meath." It was needless to add that this comfortless solution was re- ceived with applause. No sooner was the election over than they were in the midst of their registration work, and so continuous' had been the growth of the population in the division that there was an increase of 220 in the number of electors on the register as compared with last year, the one for 1892 (excluding the duplicate reeistra- tins) containing 11,756 as against 11,970 for 1893. As usual their opponents claimed that the results of the year's registration work was a substantial gain to the Unionist party, but surely they might comfort them- selves with the reflection that as Tory gains on the register had in their Case meant increased Liberal majorities at the polls they had no cause for fear, but veetured to express the opinion that, the contests of the future would, as in the past, see Mr. Biunner more securely seated as member for the Northwich Division, by the increased confidence of the constituency as ex- pressed at the ballot box. Glancing at the progress of organised Liberalism in the division, it was satisfactory to report that the Runcorn Liberal Club had just ar- ranged to purchase and had already entered into posses- sion of commodious and convenient club premises with the satisfactory result of a large accession of members. The club promised to have considerable added influence in the advancement ot Liberal principles. Since Mr. Brunner had represented this division lie had never spared himself in their service but had been " instant in season and out of season," both in his attendance in the House of Commons and his many attentions to those of his constituents who were constantly requiring his advice and assistance and in the iifforoing of facilities for obtaining information and courageously advocating those questions both in and out of the House of Com- mons, particularly affecting their constituency. He had ever shown that be instinctively preferred the public good to personal popularity, and might be truly described as- an engrained Liberal and he might rest assured that never did he stand higher in the estimation of his constituer.ts than at the present time. (Applause.) The Chairman moved, and Mr. J. W. Deakin seconded and it was carried unanimously, that the report be adopted. ACCOUNTS.

The Treasurer (Mr.E-.3-lil-n-e-r)-s-übmitted the statement of accounts for the 3 ear ended December, 1892,which,oa the proposition of Mr. Charles Patten, was adopted.— Mr. Milner stated that he WRS calling a meeting of re- presentatives from the various districts to decide upon a scheme whereby small subscriptions could be gathered

ELECTION OV OFEICERS. Mr. E. H. Moss, of Mick!lewich, was unanimously re- elected president • Mr. G. H. Deakin, chairman of the council; Mr. H. firatt, chairman of the executive ; Mr. E. Milner, treasurer ; Mr. A. Fletcher, hon. treasurer. The following gentlemen were appointed representatives .rt the council of the National Liberal Federation : Messrs. VV. Blagg, J. Rayner, J. Hulse, T.Handlev,Thos. Hulme, J. Millington, ft Brett, E. H. Mow!, H. Capes,J. M. Fells, W. Handley, J. Clarke, and A. It. Norman. Representatives to the Cheshire Liberal Federation Messrs. E. H. Moss, E. Milner, and the Secretary.—Mr. J. W. Deakin moved the following resolution :—" That the members of the council of the North wich Division Liberal Association expresses its full confidence in the Governmert in its present sincere desire to advance the welfare of the people, as evidenced by the many admin- istrative reforms of the past twelve months and the , introduction of so many popular measures in conformity ' with the pledges given at the general election. This meeting also approves of the action of the Right Hon.W. E.Gladstone in drastically dealing with the obstruction, the avowed object of which was the rejection of the great measure of justice to our sister country in opposi- tion to theverdict of the electors. That their thanks be given to J. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P., for his faithful sup- port of the Liberal party in the House of Commons, and his constant attention in advocating and advancing those local questions which affect this consti- tuency." He believed they were going to have those reforms promised them granted to the , country, because the people of the United Kingdom had distinctly and emphatically asked for them. If the House of Lords threw cut the [Tome Rule Bill he for one was thirsting to fight them. If they were te have a second chamber they should have a thoroughly representative body, who had served their country long and well in the House of Commons. No constituency was better repreiented than Northwich. Mr. Brunner had not only been faithful and consistent and been there to vote for his party and the Grand Old Man—(applause) —but he had been looking well after local affairs, lie. would be the means of bringing about the re-constitution ot that House of Lords the Weaver Trust, which would either be mended or ended. (Applause.) He trusted for many years they would have Mr. Brunner to repre- sent them. (Applause.) Mr Kniveton, of Runcorn, in seconding the resolution, said they were satisfied with their party and with their programme, which was in the direction of the people's welfare. They were satisfied with their party, because they had been put to such a test as no party had ever been tested in the English Parliament before, and they had stood true almest without exception. At the call of duty every man had rallied to the leader; the time for talking was gone aod now was the time for action. They were trying to put several important measures on the statute book and he believed they would succeed. As to the application of the closure, the Tories took out a patent in 1887 for expediting business in the House of Commons, and the Liberal party were now using it. (Laughter.) It was answering admirably, very much to the gratifica ot the Liberals and very much to the displeasure of the Tories. I Mr. W. Illagg. in supporting the resolution, said he re- gretted that their leader should have to apply it. The Home Rule measure was of vast and far-reaching im- portance, and he thought some wiser course ought to have been taken. (Mr. Brunner: "The wiser course of the Tories.") If the Liberal party had united to forego any schemes for any English measure during the present session, he believed the Home Rule Bill would have been passed through Parliament very satisfactorily to the Government.—The resolution was unanimously carried by acclamation. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., who was enthusiastically I greeted on rising, said lie should only make a very short speech that afternoon in response to the resolution they , had passed with such kind cordiality, to him, for the , reason that the secretary's very able report which had just been read, the eloquent speech they had heard from

div.head: CONVERTING THE NIGGER.
div.p: CONVERTING THE NIGGER.

I was sitting in the bar' quietly smokin' a frugal pipe, when two middle-aged and stern looking females, and a young and pretty female, suddenly entered the room. They were accompanied by two umbrellers and a negro gentleman. "Do you feel for the down-trodden I" said one of the females, a thin-faced and sharp-voiced person in green spectacles. "Do I feet for it ?" anserd the lanlord, in a puzzle Voice : " do I feel for it ?" 'Yes, for the oppressed, the benited ?" " Inasmuch as to which ?' said the lanlord. " You see this man ?" said the female, pintin her umbreller at the negro gentleman. " Yes, mann, I see him." " Yes !" said the female, I raisin her voice to an exceedin high pitch, " you see him, and he's your brother !" " No, I'm darn'd if he is !" said the lanlord, hastily retreatin to his beer casks. "And yours !" shouted he excited female, addressin me, "he is Ms') your brother." "No, I think not, marm," I pleasantly replied. • " The nearest we came to that color in our rattily was in the case of my brother John. He had the janders for several years but they finally left him. lam happy to state that at die present time he hasn't a solitary jander." " Look at this man !" screamed the female. hooked at him. He was a able- bodid, well-dressed, comfortable-lookin negro. He looked as tho' he might heave three or four good meals a oay into him without a murmur. " Look at that down-trodden man !" cried the female, " Who tred on him ?" I inquired. " Villins, despots !" " Well," said the lan'toril, " why don't you go to the willins about it? Why do you comer here tellin us niggers is our brothers, and brandishin your umbrellers round like a lot of lunytics ? You're wuss than the sperrit-rappers." " Have you," said middle-aged female No. 2, who was a quieter sort of person, " have you no sentiment—no poetry in your soul—no love for the beautiful ? Dust never go into the green fields to cull the beautiful flowers ?" "I not only never dust," said the landlord,in a angry voice, but I'll bet you five pound you can't bring a man as dares say I dost." " The little birds," continued the female," (lost not love to gaze onto them" " I would I were a bird, that I might fly to thou !" I humerusly sung, casting a sweet glance at the pretty , young woman. " Don't you look in that way at my dawter !" said female No. 1, in a violent voice ; "you're old enough to be her father." "'Twas an innocent look , dear madam," I softly said. " You behold in me an emblem of innocence and purity. In fack, I st..irt for Home by the first train to-limner to sit as a model to a celebrated artist who is about to sculp a statue to be called Sweet Innocence. Do you s'pose a sculper would send for me for that purpose onlees h know'd I was overflowin with innoe.ency ? Don't make nn error about , me." "Itis my opinyn," said the leadin female, "that you're a skoffer ant a wretch ! Your mind is in a wus- ser beclouded state than the poor negroos we are seekin to aid. You are a groper in the dark cellar of sin. 0 sinful man !
There is a soarklln fount Coale, O. coma and drink.

No ; you dill not come and drink." " Yes he will," said the landlord, "if you'll treat. Jest try him." "As for you,"said the enraged female to the lanlord," you're a degraded hein, too low and wulgor to talk t."" This is the sparklin fount or me, near sister !" cried the lan'lord, drawin and drinkin a mug of beer. Flavin uttered which goak, he gave a low rurnblin tart% and relapst into silence. "My coloured fren'," I said to the negro kindly, " what is it all about ?" He said they were trying to raise money to send missionaries to the Southern States in America to preach to the vast num- bers of negroes recently made free there. He said they were without the gospel. They were without tracts. I said, "My fren', this is a seris matter. I admire you for tryin to help the race to which you belong, and far be it from me to say anything agin carryin the gospel among the blacks of the South. Let the gospel go to them by all means. But I happen to individooally know that there are some thousands of liberated blacks in the south who are starvin. I don't blame anybody for this, but it is a very sad fact. Some are really to ill to work, some can't get work to chi, and others are too foolish to see any necessity for workin. I was down there last winter, and I observed that this class had plenty of preachin for their souls,but skurcely any vittles for their stummux. Now, if it is proposed to send flour and bacon along with the gospel, the idea is really an excel- lent one. If on thet'other hand it is proposed to send preachin alone, all I can say is that it's a hard case for the niggers. If you expect a e,loured person to get deeply interested in a tract when hiastummuck is empty you expect too mech.". I gave the negro as much as! could afford, and the kind-hearted lan'lord did the same I said, "Farewell, my coloured fren'. I wish you well, certainly. You are now as free as the eagle. Be like him and soar. But don't attempt to convert a Ethio- pian person while his stuinemck yearns for vittles. And you, ladies—l hope you are as ready to help the poor and unfortunate at home as you seem to be to help thb poor unfortunate abroad." When they had gone the lanlord kaid, "Come into the garden, Ward." And we I went and culled some carrots for dinner.—.lrtentus Ward.

THE COAL TRAD CR'S!e•
THE STOPPAGE NOTICES GIVEN.

In accordance with the decision arriveu at by '1 e coalowners at the Westminster Palace Hotel, on Fri lay the 30th June, a fortnight's notice to terininat,. con- tracts was given at nearly every pit in the Midland counties on Saturday,and unless an agreement is arrived at in the intervening fortnight work will Y‘.e stopped at all the collieries on the.. 22nd inst. The notices were tendered to the men by their employers in Yorkshire, ' Lancashire, Cheshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire. Leicestershire, Warwickshire, North Staffordshire, and Somerset. In South Staffordshire the men are working under a sliding-scale agreement, and are not at present, affected by a natiQnalmovement. In Northumberland and Durham action has not so far been taken by either the employers or the men, but it is understood to be the policy of the Federation to call out the miners of the North of England under the twentieth Federation rule and at the same time to induce them to apply for ad- vances, so as to level up the wages in all the Eng isi coalfields. In the Forest of Dean the notices had been previously tendered, and in this coalfield the men ceased work on Saturday. Appeals were made to the owne s to allow the men to work for another fortnight, so that the stoppage might take place simultaneously with that in the other coalfields. hut the owners declined to tic- cede to the proposal.

div.head: ST. IIEtENS.
div.p: ST. IIEtENS.

A meeting of delegates from all the collieries in the St. lielcns. district was held at St. Helens on Saturday night to take into consideration the threataned reduc- tion of wages. It was stated that the opinion of the men was strongly in favour of resisting the reduction. The delegates ultimately decided to take a ballot at each colliery during the present week on the question " Are 3u willing to accept a reduction of 25 per cent. in your wages?" The results are to be submitted to the Conference of Lancashire district delegates at Man- chester to be held on Monday. The whole of the 4,000 collieries employed by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., of the Haydock, Ashton, Golborn., and Edge Green collieries have received preliminary notices that their contracts of service with the firm will be terminated on the 24th inst.

div.head: HAYDOCK COLLIERS AND THE PROPOSED REDUCTION.
div.p: HAYDOCK COLLIERS AND THE PROPOSED REDUCTION.

Notices were posted at all the pits beitnging to Messrs. Iglvans and Co.. on Monday, to the effect that the exist- ing, contracts with all surface and underground hands would terminate n the 24th inst. About 4,000 men will thus be affected, and judging from the present con- dition of affairs, the men will cease work on the 28th inst., as a protest against the suggested reduction. It is the general opinion of minors that the stoppage will extend over some four or five weeks, which will enable the proprietors to get rid of their surplus stocks, and tend to send prices up somewhat, tho ultimate result being a compromise between the employer anti men on an arranged basis. Mr. R. Isherwood, J.P., miners' agent, visited Haydock on Tuesday, and had several in- terviews with the delegates. His opinion is that a strike will certainly take place, but that it will not last mere than five or six weeks.

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

The proposed 25 per cent, reduction ot miners' wages has been eagerly discussed and commented upon in the Leigh colliery district, and during the week crowdsd meetings have been held at different places in the divi- • sion. At all the meetings resolutions were unanimously adopted to resist any reduction. notices have been posted at the majority of the pits to terminate all con- tracts before the and of the month. The number of colliers that will be affected is as follows :—Asr;ley and Tyldesley Coal Company's pits, 900 ; Messrs. Bamsden and Sons, Shackerley Collieries, 700 ; Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows, and therton Collieries, 2,000 ; Hindley Green pits, 900 ; Co.,dindley Field, 200 ; Abram Collieries, 1,500; Plank-lane, 2,000 ; Vi'estleigh Coal Company, 1,000 ; Wigan Coal andiron Comnanv, 1,300 ; Bedford Colliery, 700 ; Hutton Colliery, 1,000 ; Mosley Common pits, 2,000. The majority of the colliers have for some weoks worked only three or four days per week, but with the end of the month five, and in same cases even six, days per week will be worked. The stocks at the *various collieries are fairly large. NOT rs.

Twenty-five thousand notices have been sent out by the Coal Masters' Association in the Nottingh.tin district for a reduction 01 25 per cent. in conk-re' wages. In Nottingham there is a strong determination amongst the men not t submit to the reduction, and there ia every prospect of a great strike when the notices take etT2ct on the 28th inst.

div.head: GREAT FIRE AT THE WORLD'S FAIR.
div.p: GREAT FIRE AT THE WORLD'S FAIR.
MANY FIREMEN KILLED.

A terrible fire, resulting in the death of about twenty firemen, occurred on Monday, in a cold Storage ware- house in the grounds of the W-rld'b Fair, Chicago. • The: store, which was situated near the tence in 63rd-street, half-a-mile from the nearest Exposition building, was entirely gutted. While the firemen were battling with the flames on the cupola of i lefty tower in the centre of the building, the lower portion of the structure became ignited by the falling embers and suddenly collapsed, plunging its human freight into the midst of the burning mass below. The crowd of horrified spectators who stood watching the -holocaust shouted to the other firemen at the foot of the tower to keep out of the way. The I warning, however, came too late, and five more ynen were buried under the falling mass of masonry. No damage was done to the Exposition proper. The lire originated at two o'clock in tee afternoon, in the cupola of the warehouse. This structure, which was , 200 feet in height, was built of wood, and elaborately ornamented, near the top being a lauding. The flames were first observed thirty feet above this landing, and when the firemen arrived, twenty or thirty of them climbed up to it. They were preparing to bring thrir hose into play when the flames which had made their way downwards inside the tower suddenly broke out on all sides beneath the landing. An exclamation of horror immediately went up from the twenty thousand specta- tors. Five firemen saved themselves by sliding down ; the ropes, but before their companions could follow the ropes were burnt through. The remainder were then lett huddled together on the north side of the cupola, quite beyond the reach of any other means of rescue. [be crowd, being unable to render any help, stood ' horror stricken, watching the filmes mount higher and ; higher, until the firemen were almost concealed from view. One of the men sprang from the landing far ; out into the air, but was dashed to pieces on the rod of the building eighty feet below. Four others followed his example and met with a similar fate. The upper portion of the cupola was then seen to give way, anti the remaining firemen were : swallowed up in the burning mass of timbers. Marshall Murphy, one of the most fearless officers in Chicago, escaping by sliding down a rope and jumping to the root of an adjoining building. -

The crowd which assembled in the grounds to watch the fire reached very' large proportions since during the excitement thousmds of people climbed over the fences and joined the throrg of those who had paid for admis- sion. The excitement reached its climax when the first man jumped trocn the tower. a shoot of terror went up from the crowd, women fain ed, and many men fell on their knees and prayed. The efforts of the fire brigade were almost paralyzed by tue lois of so many of its members, and the excitement was increased by the arrival on the spot of the entire ambulance corps of the city.

div.head: DISPLAY OF ENGLISH BRAVEaY.
div.p: A DISPLAY OF ENGLISH BRAVEaY.

Telegraphing on Tuesday night, the Chicago corres- pondent of the" Daily Chronicle" says t —The assistance rendered at yesterday's terrible tire by the Enlist' ex-soldiers engaged in the military tournament here is the subject of universal praise. The men, to the number of about 100 were of the greatest assistance not only in the work of extinguishing the fire, but also in helping to save the fives id those in the burning building. In con- trast to Many others present they displayed admirable coolness and unexampled bravery. Many individual acts of courage are recorded. Corporal Evans, for example, with-splendid daring, plunged twice into the burning building, and on eack occ talon rescued a man. When he emerged from the veritable furnace for the second time, which he did only with difficulty, he was greeted with enthusiastic cheers by those who had watched his courageous conduct.

div.head: FOUR MEN DROWNED IN A WELL.
div.p: FOUR MEN DROWNED IN A WELL.

Three men employed in boring for water for the Shanklin Local Board being missing at midnight on Wednesday the contractor for the work descended • the well in which they were employed to search for them. Missing his footing he fell into the water and was drowned. The lifeless bodies of the four men, including the contractor and his son, were Afterwards found in the well, and on Thursday morning they were brought to the surface. The bodies recovered are those of Mr. Thomas Parsons, inventor of the patent boring machine, of St. Helens, Isle of Wight, his son, Edward Parsons, and two workmen, named Harry Simpkins and Edward Blake, both of Godshill. It is thought that all of them were overcome by the gases suddenly escaping from the boring tube, which had pierced a derth of over 200 feet.

div.head: "LOYAL " ORANGEMEN.
div.p: "LOYAL " ORANGEMEN.

Halifax, N.S., Thuraday.—An Orange celebration took place at Shubenacadia. Halifax, on Thursday, when 10,000 members of the order vrallced in procession for the first time in a quarter of a century. Majot Hughes one of the chief speakers said he had received inquiries from thousands of persons anxious to enlist in the Ca na- dian regiment which it Was proposed to organise with the view of assisting hi ituneu in case of need. Perfect order prevailed.

THE THORNHILL COLLIERY DISASTER.

The Coroner's inquiry Into the /cause of the colliery explosion at Thornhill, by which 139 miners lost their lives, was resumed at Morphia on Tuesday, in present 0. of representatives of the Rome 011ice,the Board of Trade and the organisations both of colaery proprietors and workers. Mr. E. T. Ingham, owner of Combs Pit, ;vivo evidence cc irli regard to the appointment of Mr. W. Scat as manager in sitocession to air. Jesse Taylor, a very olw servant woo retired two months ago on account g f in- creasing years. fie stated that last Easter he received an annoymous letter to the effect that there was gas* somewhere in the,seutli endings of lila pit. He caused ' his then manager, Mr. Taylor, to inspect the pit, with the result that he received a report to the eff lit that there was no gas. Six months ago ene of his surveyors mentioned to him casually that six months before that there had been a case of gas firing, in the pit, bet the matter was then so old thst nothing was done. Mr. W. Scott, manager, said there ha.i heels no rggport of the presence of gas in the pit since his appointment. On the 14:li June, however, Amos dawkesworch, an under manager, who was killed by the explosion, told him he had seen gas. Two days later Raw kesworth informed him that the gas had disappeared. No record was made of tho incident. IVitriess stated that, so far from com- plaining about the want tif ventilation, the men had said there was so much that they were starved. Open lights were used at lice bottom of the downcast shaft. With reference to these another witness recalled an occasion on which they were stopped by Ilawkes orth fora day, safety lamps being used in their place. Mr. Parker Rhodes mentiored that an urifastened lamp had been found in a mat ,he pit rgininfe from l'ilet'Scg'ne of the explosion. It was reit suggested that the lamp had anything to do with the accident. The inquiry was adjourned. The Coroner's inquiry into the colliery explosion at Thornhill, by which 133 men and boys were killed, was concluded on Wednesday. Ole of the witnesses was Mr. George F. Beecher, a mining engineer and colliery , manager, v.- ho in the course of liis evidence made the remarkable statement that on the night of the explosion he found the air of the pit near the north workings purer than the air he was then breathing. TIP? witness added that he was on the point of leading a party of ex- plorers into the north workings, where so mans' of the dead men were afterwards found, when the order was issued from above to discontinue work tor the night. But he did not think any more living men would have been found. Other expert witn-sses disagreed with Mr. Beecher OA to the state of the atmosphere, one of them stating that had any attempt been made on Tues- day night to penetrate the regrai workings thosq, who tried it would now have been in the. churchyard. Evi- dence was given to the eff,ct that a leakageof gas had existed for some time in the down-cast shalt of the pit, and the theory advanced by the mining experts was that there had been an accumulation of gas in a trough under the landing stage oppesite one of the seams, that the gas was fired by one of the naked high's suspended just above, rind that the woodwork of the shaft burning dowuwards caused the conflagration from which so large a volume of smoke was, discharged into the work- inge. Joseph Matheson, one of the men who was found alive thirty-two hours after the explosion, stated that he and the minors engaged near him did not notice any- thing wrong until two o'clogtk, two hours after the gas had tired. The unavailimt fforts of the men to escape and their gradual prostration by tho after-damp were described by the witness, who remained conscious throughout, whilst his comrades around him were dying. At the conclusion of the oil lence the jury found that the cause of deatn was accidental. They added aik expression of their admiration of the bravery of the rescue parties, and a recommendation to the colliery proprietor to discontinue the use of naked lights in the pit.

SATURDAY. JULY 15, 1893.

TEE Opposition have this week cut Opposition. a sorry and certainly not a very creditable figure in the House of Commons. During the week the Ninth Clause of the Home Rule Bill has been under consideration This Clause deals with the representation of Ire- land in the Imperial Parliament after the granting of Home Rnle. It is an important question, one of the most important raised by the whole Bill. It might have been thought that, in dealing with such a subject as this the conduct of the Opposi- tion would have been regulated by some clear guiding principle. They might, for example, have argued for the proposal contained in the Home Rule Bill of 1886, providing for the total exeluaion of the Irish members from the Imperial Parlia- ment, for a time at least. This would have given Ireland what is known as Colonial Home Rule, which the Irish themselves were • quite ready to accept: Or, if this set Med to be too much like 'what they are pleased to call "Separa- tion," they rnigl.t have agreed to the provision for the retention of the representatives of Ireland, and then have debated with some shoiv of consistency the subsidiary ques- tions which naturally arise,as to whether Irishmen should sit at Westminster for all purposes, or simply to consider Imperial matters,and also as to the number of representatives Ireland should be entitled to return. But, so utterly without guid- ing principle are the Opposition that they managed on the same night, and with the same unanimity, to vote for diametrically opposite proposals. On Monday, Mr. :REDMOND, the Parnellite leader, moved as an amendment that the repnesentation of Ireland remain at one hundred and three aa'at present, and not be reduced to eighty as proposed by the Government. This ainendrnent,strange to say, was supported by the whole strength of the Opposition party, although Unionists are never tired of telling us that Ireland is over represented in Parliament, and that Irish questions are given too much prominence. This am endmentimuch to the chagrin of those who had expected that their unscrupulous tactics would be better rewarded, was rejected by a majority of fourteen. Then, ea if to show with how little honesty and fairness this Home Rule Bill is opposed, the same very consistent politicians soon after voted that Ireland should not be represented at all. It is hard to see what credit the followers of Mr. BAVOUR and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN' can hope to achieve by adopt- ing such methods as these. They are certainly proving one thing very conclusively, and that is the wisdom of the Government in curtailing debate Against an Opposition conducted on these lines the ordinary rules and usages\ of Parliament were absolutely impotent.

• Mn. JUSTICE GRANTHAM is some- times almost unjudicial in his out- Censure. spokennesb. On more than one occasion he has used language from the bench which seemed to be scarcely in harmony with the serene atmosphere which is supposed to prevail there. But there are those who have followed the developments with regard to the Ramsgate mur- der who entirely endorse his vigorous condemna- tion of the manlier in which the case against the local butcher, Non, has been, got up by the police. Not was brought before the Ramsgate magistrates om sixteen different days before they finally decide& to commit him to the Maidstone Assizes to take his trial on the capital charge. Yet, according to Mr. Justice GRANTHAM, who presided at those Assizes, one small sheet of note- paper would have held all the legal evidence that was adduced against NOEL, instead of .the huge pile of documents which he held up in derision before the grand Jury. Thii, of course, was, in reality, a condemnation not only of the police, but also of the local magistrates /and their legal ad- ' visers for having allowed 'so much immaterial evidence to be submitted. But the police appear to have made a mistake which is not uncommon. They seem to have made up their mind early on in the calm that Non had niurdered his wife, and all their subsequent efforts were directed towards

showing that he was capable of doing such ad deed. Mrs. NOEL was shot through with a pistol. The police did not find tb pistol, but they produced a constable 1'41: said that he had seen' NOEL WaltiNg Out 1, evening four or five years ago with a ladY b°°ra keeper. The police could not show that „ clothes were bloodstained or that he bore 81,1" e signs of a struggle, but they suggested thath'is had been guilty of impropriety in his shop. the Vile evidence was, of course, all adduced to pr°v°.ve motive, but, as Judge GRANTHAM said, " n2°°id is a dangerous thing to rely upon, and should never be taken as evidence of a crime." ltogeth,.% according to thd judge, the conduct of the Poil; Lied been most reprehensible, and he did not 00e k to think any more highly of them for havingdru,ne the bottled beer of the prisoner while roak'si investigations in his house. The bill agahis it need hardly be added after such a chargo, "- thrown out by the Grand Jury.

ALLEGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES. On Monday belore Mr. H. Wade Deacon at the Widnes Police Court, Joseph Thel wall, a middle-aged man, liv- ing at Ditton, was brought up on remand, charged with burglariously breaking and entering the dwelling-house of Samuel Smith, lamplighter, early on Saturday morn- ing, and stealing therefroin various articles of clothinv. kc:;'valued at £3. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. Sodth and his wife retired to bed about eleven °Valls in Friday night, and about two o'clock the following inc. ..- ing Smith was awakened by huaring a noise in the house. He went downstairs only partially dressed, and then lie saw the prisoner just leaving the Ii Mse with the clothing. Smith gave chase after the prisoner, who dropped several articles as he ran, and after following him to Victoria-street, he suceeedtd in capturing Thelwall,who said that he had done it because lie was hard up and his father had turned him out of the house. He was handed over to Police-constable Jennings. Prisoner had effected an entrance by timing the lock of the front door with a key in his possession.—The defence was that prisoner was insane and not responsible for his actions.-Dr. O'Keefe and three other witnesses were called to speak to prisoner's strange conduct. 'rue doctor said lie could not say that prisoner did not know the difference between right and wrong ; and prisoner was committed to Liver- pool Assiz?s, bail being refused.

RUNCORN' AND TIM SHIP CANAL. The rapid progress of the works in the neighbourhood of lluncoin continues. This week, water has been ad- mitted into the length from Old Quay to Runcorn Decks, and the depth is now many feet. From the Bridge to the Old Quay the canal has not been excavated to the requisite depth of 28 feet, but the sand will be cleared away by a dredger. Below, the canal is completed, a considerable portion having been cut through the solid rock. The task of constructing Weston Lock is proceed- ing with great despatch, and no fear is entertained but that it will he completed by September,in fact it is highly 'probable that the waterway from Eastham to Old Quay will be opened by that month. It is an interesting fact that the first full rigged ship that has navigated the canal arrived at Salt:port on Sunday. The vessel is the Avon, Captain Brady, 1,590 tons register, and had a cargo of 1,816 loads of pitchpine timber consigned to the pitch- pine Company, London. The owners are Messrs. Gib- son, of Liverpool. There has also arrived the barque, Golden Horn, 1,068 tons register, with 1,683 loads of deals from Novascotta for Harrison Robinson and Co., Liverpool, Captain Andersen ; the barque, Bessie Mark- ham, TB tons register, from Parrsboro,with 1,200 loads of deals for Harrison Robinson and Co., of Liverpool, Captain Stewart ; the barque Burnham W00d,1,283 tons register, from Parrshoro, with 2,016 lods of deals for Crosfield and Co., of Barrow, Captain Smith ; the S.S. African Prince, Captain McLennan, also arrived from the Mediterranean ports and will return with a general cargo. The KS. Wensleydale is also to take out a general cargo to the Mediterranean.

WELCOME TO THE NEW VICAR OF WIDNES. For the purpose of giving a cordial welcome to the new Vicar of Widnes, the Rev. W. Hodgson, M.A., and of preienting to the former Vicar, the Rey. G. H. Garrett, 8.D., a testimonial of regard and esteem a con- versazion4 and fruit 'banquet was held in the National School en Monday evening. A very large number as- sembled. Whilst nourishment for the body was pro- vided in choice fruit, mosic was discoursed by Mr. T. Sherratt, Mr. J. R. Lea, Miss Hilda Deacon arKi Mrs. J. Coupe for the gratification of the higher senses. Mr. R. Wade Deacon was placed in the position of chairman, and in the course of the evening made the presentation, which consisted of a splendid walnut piano described as the " Stanley Model,' with check action, bushed keys, and brass pin plate. Mr. Deacon eulogised the charac- ter and work of Mr. and Mrs. Garrett. The parish had greatly plospered and extended under their diligent care. In acknowledging the handsome gift Mr. Garrett said the five years he had spent in Widnes were the happiest in his life.—The Chairman also extended a hearty welcome to the new Vicar as a Lancashire man, as a iPtccessful organiser, as a powerful preacher and as one who had shown energy and determination and 31 capacity for hard work in the parish he had left. Pro- longed applause greeted Mr. llodgson on rising. He ap- prociated the cordial welcome and appealed to the parishioners for their sympathy and help. He liked straightforward criticism and he hoped if there was any- thing wrong they would tell him straight to his face. To be successful they must be united, and he commenced his labours in a spirit of great hopf-fulness.—Speeches were made by Mr. F. Neil, Mr. D. J. Brooks, Mr. Dwerrybouse, Mr. A. Borthwick and the Rev. W. Stan- ton Jones.

THE BIBLEY °MEETING. No Warrington Volunteers have this year pro- ceeded to Bisley to represent the local corps at the ranges there. Whether they have become dis- heartened, owing to their little success there, on previous occasions is not known, but it is certain they are considerably hampered in producing good shots by the lack of a range. the nearest being Widnes. The St. llelens Volunteers, who have a range of their own,and who are usually to the fore at these meetings, this year are represented by 19 men. The representatives for Lancashire and Che- shire at Bisley this year are not as numerous as on pr. viotis yes's°. The total number for the two cmin- ties of Lancashire and Cheshire excluding Liver- pool and Birkhenhead is less than 100 volunteers, who represent some 15,000 to 20,00) of their fellows.

The annual scholars' treat for the children attend- ing the Sunday schools at -Stockton Heath, took place on Thursday and Friday. On Thursday aboutl 6CI scholars and 40 adults,belonging to the Ebenezer Wesleyan Suaday School were conveyed in 'buses :to Frodsham. They left Stockton Heath at 930, and arrived there about 11 o'clock. About 120 scholars and friends from the Appleton Wesleyan Sunday School also went to Frodsham. Dinner and tea were provided at Mersey View. The weather was beautifully fine, and a most enjoyable day was spent. Yesterday the scholars attending Sr. Thomas' Sunday School had their annual treat. They assembled at the schoolroom about 2 o'clock, and afterwards paraded the village, the children currying banners and bannerettes. They were headed by the band of the Warrington Blue Coat School, and a lorry of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co.'s conveying a number of youngsters, brought, up the rear of the procession. Many spec- tators lined the streets, and there were many flags protruding from bedroom windows. After parading the village the scholars had tea in the schoolroom. they afterwards proceeded to one of the fields in the vicinity, where gam es were indulged in.

div.head: USES OF THE PHONOGRAPH.
div.p: THE USES OF THE PHONOGRAPH.

Dr. Nansen, who has just sailed for Christiania. for the purpose of finding the North Pole, has with him a phonograph, into which his wife has sung all his favourite songs, and into which the little baby lie has left As her only comfort has also uplifted his voice in a less musical manner. An enormous supply of provisions has been taken for this expedition—provisions that will keep good for at leaat seven years. The rope has received from America a phonograph as ;an acknowledgment for the Papal salutation he con- veyed through the instrument which was exhibited to him some time ago, by means of which he heard once more the voice of Cardinal Manning. The present will not he merely a toy, for Len MIL intends to utilise it for his correspondence, which has hitherto been dictated to Monsignore Anoeli. The secretary will henceforth take (town the words from the phonograph. The instru- ment is provided with cylinders, and the first phono- gram, it is said, went to the German Emperor to con- gratulate him on the result of the elections.

div.head: VILLAGE SETTLEMEN3 S.
div.p: VILLAGE SETTLEMEN3 S.

Tha Australian colonies are following the lead of New Zealand in starting village settlement schemes. In New Zealand most settlements have proved a great SUCCNIS, in several instances the adrances made by the Govern- ment l.eing covered many times over by the value of the improvements effected by the assisted settlers. The Minister of Lands in New South Wales (Mr. Copeland) recently introduced into the Legislative Assemby of that colony an elaborate measure for establir,hing and aiding community settlements in the country districts as a means of relieving the unemployed gilliculty in the large towns. The leading feature of the Rill is that it provides for the settlement of select communities upon the soil, and also enables allowances of money to be made to them. Thus facilities will be found for people of no means as well as for those of slender means. Each association or settlement must, it is laid down, consist of at least 24 members, and a provision is made for granting Government assistance to the extent of £240 each association. The sum will be £lO to each of the 24 settlers, and this will only he advanced on condition that the members provide a similar amount themselves. —Therefore each community will start with a sum of £4BO, which Mr. C,opeland thinks should be enough to enable them to build cottages and commence operations generally.

IHE REV. THOMAS RIPPON.

The Rev.Thoinas Rippon, Who preaches the chapo! anniversary services at Bewsey-road Wesleya Chapel, Warrington, to-morrow •(Sunday), was a well-known figure in Warrington from 1881 to 1884. He is a north countryman, being a native of Gates- head near Newcastle, where he was born about forty years ago. He entered the Wesleyan ministry at an early age, and has been stationed at a large num- ber of important circuits, including Preston, War- rington, Rhyl, and Wandsworth (London). He is at present stationed at Douglas in the Isle af Man. Be is brother-in law to Dr. Hodgson, the present mayor of Crewe. He is a very popular preacher and also lecturer. During his stay in tVarringten, he was a leader in all temperance work in the town. He co-operated heartily with ministars of other denominations, and was CS popular with their con- gregations as with his own. It was at this time that Air. Slurphy, the son of the founder of the Blue Ribbon Army, visited Warrington for a fortnight, and Mr. Ilippon was his right hand man during the mission. 31r. Rippon was also it friend to the out- lying chapels in the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, and it was largely due to his exertions that the pre- sent Sankey Bridges- Weleyan Chapel was erected in the place of the small currugated iron structure which was previously in use. It is probable that no Wesleyan minister with the possible exception of the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones. ever occupied a more prominent position ill the town than Mr. Rippon. As it is some years since he last visited Warrington, he will no aoubt receive it hearty welcome.

The Isle of Man " Examiner " says that Mr. Rippon is par excellence a young man's minister, and is heart and soul with the intellectual aspirations, and the beneficial recreations of the youth of to-day. When in Wands- worth he was elected president of a cycling club corn- posed of young men, connected with his church. He has always eadzavourcd to promote the moral and spiritual welfare of young men by preaching special isermons, and there are to-Jay many men occupying front positions in the Church and • world who in their youth were influenced by him. He has a way too of gaining the confidence of children' and he organised and conducted classes for juveniles. Ile has laboured hap- pily with Church of England clergymen, and with ministers of other Nonconformist bodies other than Wesleyan Methodists, and when in London he was a frequent visitor of the Salvation Army institutions for the raising of the submerged tenth." He raised in aid lot General Booth's scheme some £5OO. As a preacher he is far above the average. He has a good appearance, a pleasant voice; line ideas which he enunciates in lam guage that flows easily ; natural and graceful gestures and a winning, clear, and earnest delivery. He is no , cushion thumper, and evidently does not favour se nsa- tiunal preaching.

div.head: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDNNT.
div.p: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDNNT.
The Mayor ot Widnes (Alderman F. II Gossage), has issued about 350 invitations for a garden party to be held at bid. reaidence Camp Hill, Woolton, on Thursday next.
The contest in Victoria ward resulted according to anticipations. The want of interest manilested by a large number of voters is shown by the ex- ceedingly light poll.

By thirteen votes to seven the Widnes Town Council declinea to pay their employes at the gas works, the trades union rare of wages. The position appears very illogical. By a resolution carried unanimously, the Council require that all contrac- tors engaged in carrying out work for the Corpora- tion shall pay tle.ir men trades union rate of wages while they, themselves, carry on what is described knobstick shop." The titters and plumbers and the stokers are paid considerably below .the minimum fixed by the Trades Union,and Councillor Gough sought to have them raised to their proper level. The men themselves have not asked for any increase; thousands are intimate with the place say there are good reasons why the men have not done se ; andit is to Mr. Goughs'a honour that he has acted as their champion.

The dignity of labour has atm dinned into our oars until, while grumbling at too much of a good thing we have accepted it as an axiom, But Mr. Councillor Smith has brought forth another rule ; it is undignified for a Councillor to labour in a cor- poration works. Mr. Councillor Gough it appears went to the Gas Works took off his coat, and worked at the furnaces for some time in order to ascertain the conoitions under which the men had to work. It is to be hoped that at sonic future time he will give us his experiences. It is such practical men that are wanted on our public bodies, men who are of the people and are•willing to labour in the interests of the people, wit-bout fear or favour. It is well that all are not bound by the starched rule of collar and cuff. '

With all our Public Health Acts and bye-laws it appears surprising that so many insanitary condi- tions should prevail in our towns ; hut the surprise will be lessened by an incident „related by Dr. Mc- ' Dougall in his annual report to Runcorn Commis- sioners. Within the last few yeare two houses of some pretentious were built on the Western side of the town. The appearance of disease in both these houses led to an inspection of the drains by Mr. Percival, the sanitary inspector, and it was found that sewage entered freely into tlie wall cavity. Some glaring defects were revealed. The soil pipes were open jointed and untrapped ; and where traps were provided they were of a worthless character. The entire absence of syphoning and ventilation of the drains provided free scope for sewer gas to travel back Into the houses, even from the main sewer. This case, says Dr. McDougall, illustrates the need of thorough inspection ; and lie urges a more strict supervision of the houses during con- struction especially of the drains and plumbers' work. And who will disagree with him, except, maybe, the jerry builder who yet abideth in the land.

It was expected that, if there was not a row there would be a " breeze "at Runcorn Board of Guar- dians on Tuesday in regard to the school fee ques- tion at Runcorn. Quite to the contrary, the reply of the Clerk ot Runcorn School Board and the letter of the Inquiry Officer, were passed over practically without comment. Not even the severe lashings administered by Mr. Imisun had roused Mr. 13randreth, who, contrary to his practice for some weeks past, is now indulging itrm. policy of "wait." And, when the moment comes, then ye shall seel It is my sincere hope that school fees may be abolished entirely and poor ancL rich placed on the same footing in regard to elementary education.

But if our Denominational managers would follow the practice of the managers of Halton Schools the present difficulty would be solved. The tradesmen, farmers and artisans, are charged a small fee for their children ' • the children of labourers, and of widows and of the poor generally are admitted free. There appeats to be some Christianity underlying this arrangement.

The amount of discussion that some subjects receive at meetings of our public bodies is often no criterion of their importance. For instance at the meeting of Runcbru. Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday nearly a half hour was consumed in dis- cussing a proposal to pay thesum of £3 to the nurse of the small-pox hospital, to which she was justly entitled; while a proposal • adopting part three of the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890. was passed without a word of comment, although this step is of great importance in carrying out the sani- tary work of the wide district over which the Authority has control. The powers of the Autho- rity are increased in many material particulars. The clanses adopted declare it a punishable offence to allow anything to pass into a sewer which will , interfere with the free flow of Sewoge or surface water, or to turn chemical refuse or waste steam, Szc., into sewers. The Authority may also make communications with sewers for owners or occu- piers. The Act adopted also declares it unlawful to erect a new building on any ground which has been filled up with, offensive matter; or to throw or suffer to be thrown into any river, stream or water- course any cinders, ashes, bricks, stone, rubbish, dust, filth, or other matter which is likely to cause annoyance. Penalties may be enforced against off..nders. The Authority are further empowered to make byelaw/ for certain sanitary purposes, and are given greater control over lodging-houses. These are a few of the advantages accruing from Tuesday's resolution. In short the Authority is endowed with many powers of an urban authority which should result in an improved administration of sanitary affairs.

After an inspection of the plans, Mr. Tiley inquired whether the committee had anything ' further to do with the matter, providing such plans were .correct from a sanitary point of view, He did not con- , sider it wise to waste time over them with regard to ally encroachment on the main road. Mr. A. Linaker con- sidered that it was fa the Cheshire County Council to look after their own interests. whereupon Mr. 11. E. Heywood proposed, and Mr. J. M.
