div.p: THE BURTON CYCLE COMPANY.
BANKRUPTCY PROCEEDINGS.

The public examination of Walter Chatwood Burton, of the Burton Cycling Co., Warrington, was commenced at the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, before 31r. Registrar Nicholson, yesterday. Tlie liabilities were £2,495 14s. and the debtor's assets amounted to £4OO 12s.,and after deducting expenses leaves £331 18. Si. The bankrupt stated that his bankruptcy was due to , loss through fire at his works last A itzust, expenses iu ! perfecting of patents, and losses on contracts. Mr. Potter, the assistant official receiver, remarked that the receiving order was made on the debtor's own petition, and on the same dee, there was an execution in processi of levy. Judgment had been s'ened in another action, arid a farther action was pending. The debtor stated that be was a mechanical engineer by trade, and he commenced business in June 1891, as a cycle manufacturer, agent, and repairer in Foondry-st., Warrington, with a loan of £lOO. He removed about March, 1892, to larger premises in Bewsev-street, War- ringtou, and in consequence of those premises having been burnt down, removed in August, 1892, to his pre- sent premises. 'De debtor had not yet filid a deficiency account, but promised to do so shortly., He appeared up to the old of February last to have kept a complete set of books by double entry, end to have had them balanced and balance sheets made out therefrom in August, 1891, and May, 1892 ; that on the latter date skowing a net profit of £179 9s. 10d. after the debtor's withdrawals had been included under the heading "Wages." 'rime debtor had not explsined why his cash hook and lodger contained no entries after February 28th. In May the debtor attempted to float his business AB a limited com- pany. A prospectus WAR lamed stating, jitter alia, that the capital was to he £lO,OOO in 10,000 £1 shares ; the purchase money £1,500 in cash and £3,500 in fully paid up shares that the debtor was to pay all promotion money and expenses, excepting brokerage, up to date of allotment ; that the engine, shafting, tools, fixtures, stock, finished and unfinished machines at the works, has been valuesi by a mill, mschinery,and land valu-r at £1,720 ss. 34. ; and the books of accounts examined by a chartered accountant who certified that from August 29, 1891, to May 28, 1892 (nine months), taking the valuation of the stock AR appearing in the books as correct, a profit of over 25 per cent. had been made on the capital then employed in the business hut that it was not possible to give a result of the business subse- quintly, because owing to the fire and subsequent removal, the business had not been in full working order. The debtor said he had only first become aware of his insolvency %viten the company Is to go to allot- ment on June 6udi last,and alleged be had not contracted any debts with a knowledge of insolvency. 'Flip follow- ing As a classification of liabilities :.—Loans,and interest, £1,247 04. 51. ; goods supplied, £921 19s 11.; work done, £59 Si. 81. ; solicitor's,valuer's,and patent agent's clsarges' £B9 10s. 10d. ; printing and advertising, £162 18s. ; breach of contraot, £l5 ; total, £2,495 14s. The claims of the creditors folly secured almost wholly for monsy lent, was secured hy assignments by way of mortgage of the debtor's interest in a number of patents and a policy of insurance (stated to have no surrender value), a lien on a gas engine, and fittings under an agreement. And a bill of sale, dated January 15th, 1892, on the debtor's household and effects. The ere it difference between the value of the machinery. plant, and stock £1,720 3d , as valued on May Ist., and tlie value thereof £3OO was appearing in the sum- mary of the assets had not been satisfactorily ex- plained by the deliter ; he only suggested that the earlier valuation was made on Ho basis of a " going concern," the latter as a " 'molted-I.lu concern," but, apparently this was only a partial explanation. In answer to questions hy the assistalit tibia? recoi ver, Mr. Burton said that he deferred the filing of the peti- tions until there Was an execution writ against bins, because he was expecting some arra ngeinents to have a limited company. He borrowed the £lOO to commence business with from Mr. Smethurst, and was to cive him 5 per cent. proportionate interest in the bulgi- ness. The stock, etc., was valued at £BOO at the open- ing of the business. Bankrupt also admitted borrowing a:siiin of money in Jane on the security to his household furniture, for which lie guntranteed to pay 15. per ere. ; He thought that it was exhorbitant interest iii view of ' the fact that the amount borrowed was fully secured, but as lie had only loaned it for two years lie did not think so much of it. He was not as pressed for money that he had to accept a loan at any price. The reason why' he borrowed the inoney was because he re- quired capital to purchase some portion of certain foreign patents at the Crystal Palace Show, but business did not result. He also borrowed a sum of money from Mr. Knowles at 25 per cent. Security Was also given for that amount. He did not think much of the interest, as he expected ta pay the capital amount back in three months. In reply to the Official Receiver who asked the bankrupt whether he thought that his business was so flourishing that hi could pay 25 per cent., the bankrupt said that the firm were working night and day, and lie expected to realise enough on the sale of patents to clear off the debts. Ile was possessed of valu- able patents in June 1891,such as the anta-v ibrator,spindle patents, etc. They. lied since increased in value. Contitiiiing, the bankrupt stated that it was first thought of making arrangements to form the business , into a company on Ist February, when a London firm, Messrs Simdkins and Co., offered to put down deben- ture shares to the amount of £2,000. The registered capital WAR £5,500. These debentures would be sufficient to pay off the debts. The matter fell through because ths firm would not guarantee that the money would be passed over for the debentures. The valoatien ot the Plant and stock. by Mr. Noble at £1,720 ss. 21. was made on the basis of a ening concern. In forming the limited comoany of 10,000 £1 shares,be was to have 3,590 and £1,500 in cash. His shares were to receive no dividends until the business gave 10 per cent. profit. He was to be manaDer at a nominal salary. Out of the 10,000 shares offered, only 29 shares were applied for besides those which the directors took up. It wasthis fact that omused him to find rrat his in- solvency. He had paid one creditor £l2O which he owed him since that discovery, hut did not know lie was doing wrong. . . . .

Asked what his statement About holding important and responsible posdions for 18 years meant, when lie was only 31 years of sue, the debtor said that even when he was eleven years or age he wac a manager. He had cant rot of a !pimp! amount, n 1 cash, and had to do with 40 mem, This explanation led the registrar to exclaim y. in must be a %older of the world." - The exg,n!nation was illstponed until September lst, and the bankrupt was ordered to make a deticie ncy account by August 15;

James Billington, the public executioner, brought an action at thb Manchester Assizes on Wednesday, against a weekly paper called " The Spy," to re'enver damages tor libel. After eonie evidence had been heard, the judge stopped the e.se on the ground that BiHinton's eliarac ter had not been injured, and a juror was withdrawn.
MR. E. J. GUEST, J. e., &IND THE
BtEWJRS. ACTION FOR SLANDER.

At the Manchester Assize Court, yesterday, Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co„ brewers, War- rington, brought before Mr. Justice Lawrence, an action for slander against Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., Wartingto n. The action was taken upon th • following statement alleged to have been made 1, the defendant at a meeting of the Warringtou Liberal Association, held on the 21st March, last : " That was a most disgraceful scene in the Cheater Assizes the other day when a publican ought to :have had £3OO, and the great brewing company • would uot give a farthing without being compelled • todo so by law ; anti Warn glad to say they were compelled." The plaintiffs put in a claim tor £l,OOO damages, in consequence cif what they suffered from loss of credit and reputation." There was a , considerable amount of interest taken in the case both by Warrington temperance men and Manches- ter advocates. alr.Williain Roberts, secretary of the Warrington Temperance Federation, Mr. IL Storey, and Councillor Dixon were amongst the spectators. The Council for the plaintiffs were Mr. Addison, Q.c., and air. Mattinson, Q.C., (instructed by Messrs. I Robert Davies, KirConneli, 'Davies and Burgess of Warrington) and for the defendant, Mr. Sutton, QC., (instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw.) Mr. Addison, Q.C., in opening the case for the plaintiffs said that the defendant Mr. Guest, had at a public meeting used words of his clients that were untrue and calculated to injure Messrs. Greenall. Whitley hna Co. The plaintiffs were a firm of which Sir Gilbert Greenall was u partner. SbeireiGi itlhbeertratirrleiaemnaelnl thaardy for membernearl y for lt half with a few short intervals in which f 'eaa rlervei sgt uitiorolytl returned. After this half a century of work, Sir Gilbert Greenall had decided to retire, and for cer- tain reasons he converted his business into a limited company, the partners in which, were not the general public, but simply gentlemen who had had an interest in the conceit! before it was converted iuto a company. He was very sorry that politica had been brought into the case before them, but he was sure that whether the jury were in a majority as Tories or as Liberals they would place aside their political principles and deal out justice. Ths company who were his clients had a number of hotels in Warrington and St. Helens,and thus anything of an untrue character made public in the locality would particularly injure the com- pany. Now Mr. Guest had for a great many years been a very strong political opponent of Sir Gilbert Greenall. lie had not only been opposed to him , in politics,but being a very strong advocate of teeto- talism, he was naturally a strong opponent of the rights and privileges of the brewers. One could not complain of that, so long as Mr. Guest kept ' within bounds when denouncing what he might term his fellow townsmen. Mr. Guest himself lived labout 12 miles out ef IVarrington, and he was a , 1 borough magistrate, aad therefore ought to be able to guard his words, and especially to be careful and guarded when dealing with his political opponents, where tneir pri ante , business was concerned. In any case of that char- acter every eenaitive man—he would not say honourable man—ought to be extremely careful in dealing with the commercial conduct ut his politi- cal opponent, even more so than lie would be with : his awl' friends. On the 21st March ut a meeting held at the Warrington Liberal Club, Mr. Guest 1 .delivered a speech containing the slander corn- pleined of. Tate passage in the speech which was in question was this: 'That was a most disgraceful beetle in the Chester Aatizes the other day al hen a publican ought to have had .£lOO and the great brewing company would not give a farthing with- out being compelled to do so by the law, and I am glad to say they were compelled." In that passage there were grave imputations made, when it was said that a firm would not pay a farthing of their lawful debts until brought into Court and compelled. The imputation had been so grave that sir Gil- bert Greene!l and his partners conld not rest under it. There had been no such claim as thedefen- daut had named made against the plaintiffs ; they haul never been compelled to pay £lOO, and never been asked. The whole affair seemed to have arisen out of an action heard before Mr. Justice Cave, at the Cheater Assizes. The company had an hotel known as the Wynnstay Arms, at Ithyl, worth about £5O a year. In February 1892 a man named Baldwin was granted the tenancy at £lO per year, and the plaintiffs paid rates and taxes, but tile tenant had to purchase his beer and stout from the plaintiffs; lie could purchase his spirits and wipes where lie chose. There was no I sort of goodwill ; they took nothing from the in- coming tenant and gave nothing to the outgoing tenant,and upon the beer they only charged invoice price so that the tenant had all profit from retail sales. The tenancy was a twelve months' one, ter- minable at three months' notice, but a tenant was always allowed to continue no long as he conducted the business respectably. In July, Baldwin, for ; some reason gave notice to lave, and desired theft the tenancy should be handed over to a Mr. Clough and eventually the plaintiffs- agreed to take Mr Clough. In the mean:IUDS Baldwin had made a pri- vate arrangement with Clough, for £lOO as ingoing money,and this was a transaction which the Brew- ery Company kite ei nothing of, and had nothing to do with. After entering tile house, Clough would not pay Baldwin the .1:100. and consequently Bald- win took up the acti fit. One of Clough's witnesses wits It traveller for the Company, maned Hartley, and whilst examining him, Mr. Justice Cave had asked if Green/ill and Whitley did nob compensate outgoing tenants for eoodwill ; the traveller who seeined confused at the question said them was no goodwill recognised by the Brewery Company, tied in further r uswer to a question said "No, the breviery do not pay for compensation for goodwill." This had caused JuA4.le Cave t.a be under .t misappre- hension, and he spoke reprehensively of any brtwery company refusing to pay guodwil.. This statement was made in ignorance of the true arrangements which ex- hated between the Company arid their tenants. Mr. Guest seemed to have taken his text. from this, and stated that Messrs. tireettall anal Whitley ware the de- fendants in the action and were compelled to pay £lOO. this had tv-en a very serious reflection and slander upon their reputation, and was without an atom of truth. The Stfttrl»tliit, too, was all the more serious as it cone upon tie authcrity of a Justica of the Peace, who taught to have read Justice Cave's remarks more carefully than the general public. Sir Gilbert Greenab, and Mr. D iwns, his manager, who was the defendant's brother-in-law, were considerably annoyed upon reading the defendant's statement, but gave him ample oppertuuity to apoloaise. Oat that 23rd March the plaintiffs' solicitors, Messrs. • It. Davies Kirkeonnell and Company, forwarded a letter to the defendant calling attention to his statement. The letter 'concluded :--e We must therefore call upon 'oil (thqugh we regret to have to write to you on smith term') to withdraw your accusation and to consent to apologise publicly for having made it." In reps' to this the tollowing letter was received from Mesas. P. Davies and 'Fawshaw : "Dear Sirs, Mr.EavrinJ.Guest has consulted us upon your letter to him of the 25ed inst, and in reply thereto we beg to state that our client regreta hiving stated that the greet brewing first were compelled to pay £lOO to one of their outgoing tenants as lie tit& that it was not true. What lie had an his tnitid at the time was what Jlistice Cave stated in the case to erred to in your letter i.e that it would be en outrage( us and monstrous thing that a brewer should by his conduct confiscate an increased value, brought about by the work of the tenant and it was all the more outrageous in face of the fact that brewers were going upend down the country complareine, that their property was being Confiscated. If there was to be any confiseation at all he (the judge) would much prefer to see the brewers' property confiscated by Government than to see the brewers confiscate the property of their tenants in this way.' However our chent regrets haviag made the mistake andapologizes for it.—Yours, Percy Davies and Fawshaw." Other correspondence took place hut the defendant consented simply to the foregoing letter being published as an ample atehogy. The plaintiffs refused to accept this as it was accompanied by something which vroold have appeared to justify the standar to some extent, but which was also the outcome of a mis- take. Mr.Thornas John Down, Managing director, to Messrs. Greeuall, Whitley, and Co., was called, and stated that his firm were in no way connected with the case at Cheater Assizes and had never been coin:wiled to pay £.1.00,t0 any one. It was aPo a fact that goodwill was nut ." • • - there was no such thing recognized by his Laitats , that , In connection with their houses. It. was a fact that they had about 700 hoasee itt Warrington and St. llelens, and the defendant's sia'ement was likely t) injure them. Mr. Sutton Q.C. (for• the defence) ; Did you mvr think of denying the statements made about the good- will.—Yes, I did so.—When did you do it P—l wrote to the papers--When did you write ? In April !—And the statement had been made a month before.- Why, did you not write earlier ?—llecause private matters prevented me. Mr. Justice Lawrence : rhis wit do the defence no gond. When a man has made a mistake like Mr. Guest had done he ought to have given as much publicity to the apology as tha statenient obtaineti.—Mr. Sutton : But lie had been misled.—lt does not matter. although Mr. Guest might have made the statement in excite- rnent-.—and both parties are often guilty of wild speaking there came calmer moments after-

wards when he ought to have seen and admitted his mistake in a proper manner.—But we do admit the mistake and have done so, only we want to prove that Mr. Guest was misled owing to Mr. Justice Cave's retnarks.—lt does Not matter v, hat Mr. Justice Cave said ; judges often make mistakes. I have made mistakes, and so have others, and it does not matter how broad Mr. Justice Cave's shoulders may beer how good a man he may be; there was no doubt he mad. , a mistake which was owing to the stupid answer made ta him by the traveller wh evidently did not understand what was meant by compensation lor goodwill.—But we ~ffered an apology in the first letter to the plaintiff's solicitor That was not a true and straightforward apology such as they required, and the best thing to do in a case when one knows he is wrong is to apologise openly and without restraint. After a further discussion, Mr:" Justice Lawrence asked if the plaintiffs wished to claim heavy damages. After a brief consultation with his colleague, Mr. Addi- son said they would accept forty shillings and coats and ! an analogy.

M. Sutton accepted the terms on behalf of the defen- dant, and said Mr. Guest was willing to express his sorrow at having made the mistake.—Before referring to the jury for their consent, Mr. Justice Lawrence said the matter right through seemsd to be one of misappre- hension, hut he thought it was a necessary thing for a man when speaking of his political opponents to use caution, and there was no place where more wild talk was indulged in than on the platform, and he could say that after experiencing it.—A verdict for the plaintiff's for 40.3. and 'costs was then given.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

1 Some revolting circumstances came to light at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, when a man named John Dillon and his wife, who resided in Ship-yard, were brought before the magistrates on the charge of neglecting their children. Their child of seven months only weighed B}lbs., and it was covered with tilth,and sucking through a vile-smel- ing tube horn a bottle in which there was some bread and water which had gone sour. Their other two small children were also seen by Inspector Up- hill, N.S.P.C.C., under most disgusting circum- stances, lying on a rotten mattress, and in a stench that was almost unbearable. This was not a , case of hopeless and helpkss poveity. As it was, the an gets 245. a week in wages and a quarterly pension that amounts to 2s. per week. The real cause was not far to seek, and it is the same cause that is at the root of so many other evils, that is, drink. The man, instead of looking after his family, appears to hare treated the whole of the Ship-yard inhabitants with the money he received from his pension. Such parents as these deserve a heavy punishment,and a month's imprisonment was none too long. Mr. Di

Aim Diggle did not make much impression upon his hearers on Monday night at his lectures on sanitation. 11e tried to frighten them by saying that tho town is in danger of another epidemic of smallpox, and other frightful things, if the Health Committee and the Sanitary Works Committee do net mend their ways, and accept the help he offers so freely. But the audience, did not appear to appreciate the gravity of the situation. They took it all as a joke, and when Mr. Diggle plaintively beggeu for a vote of thanks, he was unable to get any thanks whatever. Poor Mr, i iggle ! He has learned that a prophet has no honour in his own town. He claims that he is a philanthropist, and that on that ground alone is he advocating his views, as, he says, if they were adopted now, he will not live to receive the benefits from them. This philanthropy, however, is wasted upon tbe people of Warrington to judge from the reception he gets when lie endeavours to obtain their suff- rages,ard. as he only got 12 and 14 retes in his own w the Council. at the last times he endeavoured to get into

A certain Nonconformist congregation in town were on Sunday last either the victims of a playful jeston the part of the minister,or he was the victim of a little amusing oversight. The local minister ought to have preached, but in his place in the pulpit appeared a stranger,whom no one seemed to know. Just before the sermon the minister seemed to realise that he was the object of a considerable amount of speculation, so he delivered himself thus :—" Being a stranger here,' think I owe you a little explanation as to who I am. Last week I wrote your minister and asked him if he would preach the children's anniversary sermons at my chapel, and he consented on tile condition that I tilled his pulpit. This I consented to do, and I feel very much pleased with Warrington, upon my first visit." Then apparently all unconscious of having omitted his name, and what someone playfully chlled his "come from," the preacher went on with his sermon, leaving the congregation just as much in the dark as before.

Now this reminds me of another little misunder- standing which occurred a few weeks ago at a chapel certainly within the proverbial one hundred miles of Warrington. It was a very close evening. One of the members of the congregation handed np a note to the minister with the following on it "Give us short meter to-night." This was meant to be a request that the service and sermon should be shortened. But the minister innocently passed the note on to the organist,being under the impres- sion that short meter was required in the musical portion of the service. The organist demurred fora time at. having to alter his selections,but eventually he was persuade-I by the minister to select hymns of a short meter. it is supposed that the minister did not see the hint. Perhaps not—maybe he didn't care to.

You commented last week upon the demoralisa- tion caused in Switzerland by strong drink, and, on the Rattle gubject,l notice that it is now stated that 50,000 school children in England examined by doc- tors more than 30 per cent. were found suffering from physical or mental defects, largely attribut- able either directly or indirectly to the drinking habits cf their parents. In Belgium the Govern- ment have caused the following placard to be hung up in every schoolroom :—" Of one hundred and twenty-five thousand deaths, as many as twenty- five thousand, or one-fifth, are the result of alcoho- lism. In a period during which the population has increased by fourteen per cent., the consumption of alcohol has been augumentEd by thirty-seven per cent.,cases of madnesS by forty-five per cent.,crimes by seventy-faur per cent, suicides by eighty per .tent..and vagrants and beggars by one hundred and fifty-six per cent." • Awful though such facts are, they cannot be too well-known, and our govern- ment at home might do many a worse thing than have some of our own social statistics thus dangled before the eyes of the rising generation. MERLIN.

div.head: BOATING ACCIDENT AT SKEONESS. A WARRINGTON MAN DROWNED.
div.p: BOATING ACCIDENT AT SKEONESS. A WARRINGTON MAN DROWNED.

On Saturday afternoon, a boating disaster occurred off Skegness, in which twenty-six men lost their lives. A party of workmen in the employ or the North London Railway uompanv at Acton,. left London in the morning for a day's outing at Skegneas. Twenty-seven of them hired a yawl— the Shannon—for a sail and two boatmen accom-' panied thest. On returning at one o'clock itt the afternoon, the boat was capsized by a sudden gust of wind, and the whole of the party were thrown,. into the sea, and only three of them were saved. Twelve bodies o,ere recovered. The first name on the list of those drowned, published on Monday morning, was Mr. Ilawkins,aecretary of the Clapton Social Club, and aged 50 years. It was subsequently di.covered that this person was Mr. William Hawkins, aged 39 years, son of Mr. Vig.S. Hawkins, registrar of births and deaths, and late assistant overseer of Latchford. There will he much sympathy extended towards Mr. Hawkins, as LW loss has happened under very painful circumstance Mr. Hawkins, sen., had been during the past month in very delicate health, anti his son had been with him the whole of the time. As Le improved'sorae- whet, the son returned to business, and there joined the Skegness trip. The deceased gentleman was the second son of Mr. W. S. Hawkins, and has been engaged for some years as an Assurance Agent in London. He was also secretary of a number of other societies, amongst which was the Clapton Foinl Club, from which 13 members joined thetrip oconieSoaft uwr dh lie leaves san infant a owf widow foeww andmonfitvhes

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
Too SHARP FOR THE POACHER.

George Sefton, 3, Back Stamford-st., was returning home with his mate, early on Thursday morning, the 29th June, with a bag on his back, which contained the return for his night's labours, namely three rabbits. It was at 2.15 when they reached Winwick-road, and it was then that they were espied by P.C. Newey, who secreted himself until they came up. On seeing the officer they immediately bolted, but the officer was too quick for Sefton and caught him. To use the officer's own words "knowing that Sefton *as a man who earned his living by poaching" he asked him Vi hat he had in his bag to which he replied "a rabbit or two." The bag was examined and three live rabbits were found, along with some nets and pegs. They were brought to the police station, and on Monday Sefton was fined and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. ALLEGED DRUNKENNESS IN A PUBLIC-HOUSE. _ _

At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, George Crawford, publican of the Old House at Home, Friar's Green,was charged with unlawfully permitting drunken- ness on his premises on the Ist inst. Mr. Percy Davies de- fended.—Detective Monaghan, said that at seven o'clock on Saturday night he visited the Old House at Home, and saw three women and two men in the tap room. He noticed that there was a jug and a glass of beer on the table. One man was very drunk and fast asleep on the seat. Witness .pformed the landlady and woke the man. Ile:afterwards went out and brought r.c. Nlahay. They met the man in such a drunken condition that was locked up and fined the next day.—Dy Mr. Davies: He never saw the prisoner drink any beer.—Margaret Crawford and Isabella Crawford, were each called to prove that prisoner came into the house.but was refused any drink as he was drunk. They put him out and he must have come in again, but they did not see him come in nor serve him. A witness, Doutiyic McGowan. also corroborated the evidence for the defence. The magis- trates dismissed the case. OVBRCROWDING wint LODGERS. '

At the Borough Court on Monday, Thomas Harrison, 4, Warburton-at., was charged with keeping lodgers on the 28th June, without having had the house registered. Inspector Norman prosecuted. He said the defendant's house was visited by Inspector Powell,who found twelve persons living there. The house was in a most filthy condition. The case was reported to the Health Com- mittee, and it was decided to allow him a short time to get rid of them. But instrad of doing so he increased the number to thirteen. The house was a perfect pig- sty, and it was no wonder that the town was troubled with smallpox and other diseases. Inspector Powell said he visited the house en the 28th June. In the front bedroom he found a woman and four children in the same bed. In the same room there was a man sleeping on an old mattress, which was rotton throagh. The other bedroom was also crowded. Several persons were also sleeping downstairs. A girl aged 15 had been put under the stairs where coal was kept in order that lie might not see her. The landlady came downstairs quite drunk. He told the defendant and he said it was his wife's fault, and it would serve her right if she was sent to gaol. The nenee was very dirty. The magistrates fined the defendant £2 and costs or one month's imprison- ment.

div.head: UNJUST SCALES.
div.p: UNJUST SCALES.

At the Warrington Borough Court Monday, John Richard Lilley, living at 5, Pitt-street, was charged with having on the 26th of June. a weighing machine which was unjust. Mr. J Lyon Whittle, (town clerk) prose- cuted. He said the defendant had a shop in Pitt-street, -off Bewsey-road, and was also employed by Mr. J. Kenworthy, timber merchant. The premises of the defendant were visited by Inspector Crabtree, who found a pair of scales nine ounces against the purchaser. —lnspector Crabtree said he vis,ted the defendant's place of business, and asked if they had any scales to which the defendant's wife replied in the negative. He afterwards saw a boy wheeling a coal- barrow and found that it belonged to the defendant. He went to the back premises and found a coal-yard and a weighing machine. He examined it but found it did not work properly, and was two pounds against the owners. He afterwards found that two washers bad been placed in the machine which stopped it from working freely. 'they must not have been there long as it was impossible to weigh anything viith the machine+. When he pulled the washers out he found it was nine ounces against the purchaser. The defendant's wife could not give an account of how the washers got there. The magistrates fined the defendant LC and costs or one month's • im- prisonment.—Michael McCoy, shopkeeper, 53, Pierpoint- streets was charged 'with having a scale unjust. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle said the scales were found to be wrong to the extent of twelve drams against the purchaser. In- spector Crabtree said he visited the defendant's shop and the scales seemed as if a piece of lead had been bored out of the scale which made it twelve drams against the purchaser. Mr. E. Place, Market Inspector. said be examined the scales himself six months ago and they were then right. He thought it was a case of neglect, rot of wilful fraud. The defendant was fined the cO3tB 75.

before Mr. John fairclough (in the chair) and Alderrmin Chandley„ Ann Bendell, wife of James Brndell, lodging at Daley's lodging house, was charged with stealing a &beet, value 3s. 2d. Prisoner was also charged with attempting to commit suicide in the police cells. Mr. Hunt said Mr. Daley handed a pawn-ticket for a sheet to .I?.C. Clarke, wkich had been pledged at Mr. Jackson's Church-street. It was ascertained that the daughter of ' the prisoner had been sent to pledge it by her mother. The prisoner was brought to the police station, and searched, when a table knife was found upon her. Soon after being locked up P.C. Baxendale went to the cell and found a handkerchief tied very securely round her neck. It was with some difficulty he untied it, and it was with some time before she came round. She after- wards told Sergeant Chantler that she did not intend to steal the sheet. She pawned it in order to get some- thing for her husband's dinner, and that she " would have been a dead un " had not the officer stopped her.

James Daley said the prisoner's husband. ever since he came to live at his house had been a hard-working man. The sheet had been pawned by the prisoner for the purpose of getting drink. The children were never short of food. Her husband dare not give her money as she west to the public-house. The Bench were of the opinion that drink was at the bottom of it all, and sent her to nrison for 14(days. AN UNHAPPY MAnnianE. James McCarthy. was charged at the Borough Court. on Wednesday. with having on the 19th June unlaw- fully assaulted and beaten his wife. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. My. A. Browne represented the plaintiff. He said the prisoner was summoned to appear previ- ously, but did not put in an appearance. The defendant was a striker at Mr. Long's tannery, 'I helwall, and earned from 28s. to 325. per week. He was married in 1887. but his wife, owing to his conduct, had lived four years away from him. On the 19th June the defendant instead of going to his work returned home drunk, and attempted 0 choke his wife. She afterwards went out and he locked the door against her, and she went to her sister's house. On the following day he sold the furni- ture, and had spent the money in drink. On the Satur- day night previous to this assault she had to fight him the whole night to keep him from throttling her, and when she spoke to him of his conduct the next morning, he filled his mouth with milk and spat it on her face. He asked for a separation order. Mrs. McCarthy corro-

hrirated Mr. Browne' s statement.—Mrs. Stcckton, mother of the complainant, said she had provided them with two houses of furniture. Her daughter had been unable to live with McCarthy, and had left him several times. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for 14 days, and made a separation order, the prisoner to contribute 10a. per week towards the maintenance of his wife and child. DAMAGING GROWING OATS.

At the Borough Court, yesterday, four youths named Joseph Brooke 4 (10), 4, Siddall-st. ; Albert Dagnall (13), Robert Carty (12), and Walter Hudson, living in War- burton-st.. were charged with doing aamage to growing oats in afield near tolirinwick-road,to the extent of 45., the property of James Robinson, Avenue Farm, Orford. Prisoners pleaded guilty. Mr. J. D. Buckton, solicitor, represented the complainant. He said boys were con- tinually getting over the fences of the field, and doing damage there. The oats were being continually trodden down and being pulled up by boys to feed fowls, rab- bits, ism, with. Mr. Robinson bad driven them off three times that morning, but Gould not catch them. One of his men afterwards caught the boy Brookes. They seemed to be utterly regardless to anything, that complainant to'd them. The magis- trates fined each defendant Zs. 8d .and costs, and ls.each the damage, which amounted to 7s. each.

THEFT FROM A PROVISMN SHOP.—Mary Leicester, 24, Percivals-fold, was charged with stealing a tin of corned beef and a pound of cheese valued 23. from the Liverpool shop in Butterrnarket-st., on Saturday night. Prisoner had bought some pepper,and on going out,while another customer was being served,Edward Green, the manager of the shop heard the noise of the tins being disturbed. Be noticed that a tin was missing, and went out and informed P.S.Taylor, who searched prisOner's house and found the tin. Some cheese was also identified as belonging to the shop. Prisoner was fined 103. includ- ing costs or seven days. riE OBJECTED TO BRING TOLD ABOUT ma WAISTCOAT.— Richard Brindley, Goulden-st.,was charged with assault- ing Gerrard Jackson Rathbone, son of Mr. Andrew Rath- bone,43,Arpley-st.,cat Friday morning. Mr. Percy Davies who prosecuted said that Rathbone was standing by watching a boy named Kent light a fire near Trinity Schools. Defendant was also there, and Rathbone noticed that his waistcoat was unbuttoned and told him so. Upon this defendant picked up a piece of brick and thing it at Rathbone,hitting him near the eye. The blow knocked him on the ground and he was picked up un- conscious, and he had been under Dr. Joseph ever since. It was shown that defendant was a butt to other boys, though it was proved that no stones were thrown at him on the present occasion, and as Mr. Rathhone did not press the case, the magistrates fined him 53. including costs.

Constable Corbett said he, was in company with P.C. Lewis, and found the two defendants OR the top of a haystack. A quantity of hay had been thrown from the tof the stack in order to make A bed. Asseuvrs.—Jessie Mechin, 57. Orford-street. was charged with assaulting Annie Fletcher, lodging at 37, Price-st., on the 11th July. From the evidence it ap- peared that the defendant came to the complainant for some arrears of rent due, but not receiving them, a scuffle ensued in which Mrs. Mechin knocked the com- plainant to the ground, and trampled on her, and knocked her head against the wall. For the defence the prisoner pleaded that the complainant was the first to strike, and that she struck her back in self-defence. The magistrates bound the dsfendant over to keep the peace for six months in her own recrignizances of £s,and to pay the costs,l7s.—Kate Da lton,Dial-st.,was charged with assaulting Harriet Mills, Dial-st., on the 7th inst. Mrs. Dalton said she went to look for her boy when she was met by the defendant who struck her on the head with a cricket bat. It transpired that there had been a quarrel between the two, and the magistrates dis- missed the case.

WARRINGTON v. SALL—The first meeting ot these clubs this season took place at Arpley on Saturday, before nearly a thousand spectators. Whilst Warring- ton lacked the services of Mr. R. Smith, the visitors were short of Mr. C. H. Benton, both these players doing duty for Lancashire 2nd against Worcester. Sale started and came on for 132 runs. Warrington com- menced in promising fashion, and although S. M. Cros- field was early let off, he afierwards scored freely. Another escape at 40, at the hands of Royle, was followed by a wild return from C. E. Browning turning a single of Griffen's into five; but the aggregate reached 58 Wore S. M. Crostield was beaten by Whitelegge. Wright, who had relieved Browning, opened extremely well with a series of maidens, but Whitelegge was more fortunate than the new trundler, for at 60 he also bowled J. J. Crosfield. With Sogg as Griffen's partner runs came freely, the professional hitting Wright for 13 in two overs, but the Sale professional had his revenge on Griffen an over later, that playerretting his leg It, front of a straight one. Three wickets were thus down for 92. and sixteen runs were added when Sugg was," yorked Two runs later G. Clarke, Clark, and Reynolds were all sent back, and Jefferson being run out (a questionable decision) Parry did net trouble the scorers, and voisey , being absent the innings closed for 119, being a minority 1 by 13 rms. Wrrumovon.—The last stage In the championship competition prior to the semifinal was disposed of on SatUrday on the Griffin Green at Lower Broughton. Both the contestants have pre- viously held the championship, Newton in 1990, and Withington in the year previeus. Play opened with an exciting battle between the Newton captain and R. Williamson, which was settled by a single shot in favour of the Midland. At quarter-time, mainly owing to an unfortunate single return by Henry Sampson, Newton had run nine points to the fore, three of which Withing- ton recovered in the next two rounds. A haul of 15 by E. Thomas was the means of reversing the lead, and at half-time the score sheet displayed Withmgton 103, Newton 91. points. In the second half of the game New- ton put in four wins against a couple by their adver- saries, but returns of the losing players were sufficiently on the road to genie to .mable Withiugton to win by a narrow majority. 208 2: • ACCIDENT IN A ST. HELENS BRICKWORKS. ACTION FOR DAMAGES.

At the St. Helens County Court on Wednesday, his Honour Judge Shand and a jury heard an fiction under the Employers' Liabnity Act. Jane Linton, aged twenty-four,spinster, sought to recover .£62 Ss. from the Roughdale Brick and Coal Company, Limited, for damages for injuries sustained on the 17rli March in the defendant companyle works. Dr. O'Feely (instructed by Mr. J. P. Mearns, St. Helens) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. G.Steel (instruicted by Messrs. Bateson and Co. Liverpool) defended. Plaintiff had to fill the press-box of a brick or drain-pipe making machine with clay, during which the crusher came down upon and smashed her right hand. It was alleged that a man named William Leather, who was entrusted with the management of the machinery, had pulled a lever without any warning, which brought down the crusher. Three fingers of her hand had to be removed in consequence. For the plaintiff it Was con- tended that the defendants were guilty of negligence in not providing proper appliances for carrying on the work—viz., pallets to feed the press-box, and In not taking Droner and ordinary means for guarding and fencing off the press-box and the scrap tables around the same. Plaintiff, Sarah Owens, and Annie Di ngsdalf, who were employed at the works at the time of the accident, alsogave tvidence.—Mr. Steele submitted that there was no case to go to the jury. Regarding neglig- ence! by Leather, the Act only provided that negligence could be alleged against a superintendent who did no manual work.--Liis Honour ruled that no evidence had been given as to Leather being a superintendent only, and be only question to go to the jury was the one about the faulty machine.—Mr. William Johnson Cook, part- ner in the firm of Robinson, Cook, and Co., engineers, St. Helens, said the machine was erected by that firm. It was the best machine that could be made for the pur- pose. By Dr.,O'Feely : The machine was twenty years old. Improvements had since been made in other parts of these kinds of machine, but not with regard to the pressers.—William Leather, who worked the machine, and Annie Cahill, who had worked at the Dress-box for several %Tare, each said the machine was not dangerous. —The jury found for the plaintiff, and awarded £2O damages, costa to fonow.
SCHOLARS TRIP FROM EARLESTOWN.

The annual excursion and treat given by Mr. Thos. Molyneux, to the children attending the various day schools in Earlestown and Newton,took place on Thursday to New Brighton. It is unner- stood that only those scholars who have not been absent from school on any single occasion except through sickness, can participate in the trip.which is appropriately named the " School children's good attendance trip." The number of scholars who qualified was 851, spread over the following schools St. Peters, Newton, St. Peters, Gas-st.; Wargrave, Vul- can, St. Mary's and St. Johns It.C., Wesleyans, St. John's mixed and infants. Accompanying these were four masters, seven mistresses, 48 teachers, two mana- gers, and 90 parents. For their: conveyance a special train was requisitioned, and very early in the morning, Children could be seen wending their way to the various schools, where they were instructed to muster about eight o'clock. On arriving at the HeilOGN, each scholar was supplied with a bun and a quantity of nuts, and shortly after eight o'clock, they made their way in pro- cession to the station. The St. Peters scholars joined the train at Newton, at 8.15, and the remainder of the schools entrained at Earlestown. By 8.25 all were aboard, rain then falling heavily, which consider- ably damped the expectations of the children. After passing Broad Green, however, the rain cleared off, and the remainder of the day, although dull was fine. On arrival at Lithe-street the children were marshalled in procession, four deep, and in this order marched through the town to the landing stage, where they embarked on one of the Wallasey Ferry boats for New Brighton,which was reached soon after 10 o'c:ock: The youngsters quickly spread themselves over the sands, but a pod number made their way to the Palace, where they were amused by a ventriloquial and conjuring entertainment, They all mustered in the Palace at 12 o'clock for dinner. During the afternoon another entertainment was given and at Ave o'clock tea was served, after which the chil- dren were kept within the building until close on six o'clock when they set out for the boat. Phey left Lime- street at 7.15, and arrived home a little before eight o'clock, after a thoroughly enjoyable out. It is pleasant to record that although such a large numoer of children of all ages from 5 to 13 years were with the trip, not a single mishap of any kind occurred.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

The House of Commons again went into Committee on ,he Home Rule Bill on Monday, resuming consideration 4 clause 9, which relates to the question of Irish repre- •entation in the House of Commons. Mr. J. REDMOND InoVed IO omit sub-section 1. so as to retain the Irish representation in full. Mr. GLADSTONE said the Govern- ment proposed that the number of Irish members should oe reduced from 103 tc 80. They meant to stand fiNs on heir proposal, and he beaten upon it if the House thought fit. The amendment was rejected by 280 to M. Mr. HERBAGE moved an amendment to exclude Ireland from representation in the House of COMMORS on the establishment of Home Rule. After a long discussion, to which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was the principal contribu- tor, a division was taken, with the result that the 'Amendment was rejected by a majority of 31.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, the Ilouse again went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, resuming consideration of section 9. Sir J. Lunnocx moved an amendment to make the number of Irish representatives in the Imperial Parliament contin- gent on the amount of the Irish contribution to the Imperial expenditure. After a long discussion it was withdrawn by leave. Sir C. Dugs moved a verbal Amendment to the clause in order to show that the Government scheme aggravated the inequalities of representation. He did not wish the amendment to go to a division, but a division was challenged from the Opposition side, and the result was a Government majority of 30. Mr. &row KARR moved an amendment to reduce tbe Irish representatives at Westminster to 48. In the ' course of the discussion on this amendment, which was defeated by a majority of 33, Mr. SEXTON spoke of a phrase of Mr. Brodrick's as " grossly imper- tinent," And, refusing to apologise, was ordered to withdraw from the House for the remainder of the sitting.

The Grand Committee of the Souse of Lords on Tues- day completed their consideration of the Places of Worship (Sites) Bill. Lord SANDFORD proposed to amend clause 11 in order that the clause might -declare that if under the bill land should at any time cease to be used as a site for a place of worship or a minister's house it should revert to its original owner. The amendment was, however, rejected. WhBNESDAY.

In the Efouse of Commons on Wednesday. Mr. Iluxzott replying to Sir CHARLES DILEE, stated that the Govern- ment had received no information as to the news from Newfoundland concerning the seizure of stores intended for French traders.

Afterwards Mr. Serros called the SPEAKER'S atten- tention to the scene on Tuesday night in order to ask in what mode he could most speedily obtain the judgment of the House on the conduct of the Chairman of Commit- tee in dealing with him under a standing order which, he urged, could tot be applied to his case, and the result was that the lion. member gave notice of a motion on which the question will again come before the House. The House went into Committee on the Horne Rule Bill, the discussion on the amendment by Mr. Parker Smith to retain the representation of Dublin University being resumed by Mr. D. Plunket. The quest ion occu- pied the attention of the House for a considerable time, and in the end the amendment was defeated by majority of 32. Mr. GLADSTONE followed with an 'im- portant statement with regard to the retention of Irish repusentation at Westminster. A point had, he said, now been reached at which it was possible to gauge the general sentiment of the House with regard to the ex- tent of the powers to be exercised by those Irish repre- sentatives who came to the Imperial Parliament. Reten- tion for all purposes appeared to be the decision arrived at, not in one quarter, but in several quarters of the House. Ira view of this fact the Governmant had de- cided to'svithdrw aih-sections 3 and 4 of clause 9,defin- ing the voting powers of the Irish members. Ho moved that these sub-sections should be omitted. Mr. RAVl- nose and Dr. WALLACE spoke in opposition to the PREMIER'S proposal, and the proceedings were adjourned while the latter was speaking. THURSDAY

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening in re- ply to Mr. J. REDMOND, Mr. GLADSTONE aiil the Govetn- ment had gladly acceded to the postponement of any attempt to fix defihitely the financial relations between Great Britain a'nd Ireland, as their information was totally insufficient for the purpose, and it was their in- tention that a Royal Commission should inquire into the subject. The House again went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, and discussion was resumed on the Pitsranta's amendment to strike out of clause 9 the sub- sections (3 and 4) relating‘to the" in-and-out "scheme. Mr. GLADSTONE, Mr. Baltonr, Mr. Chamberlain, and Sir W. tarcourt took part in the dehate,which was closured at ten o'clock. The amendment was carried by 325 to 298—majority 27. Clause 9as :intended was added to the bill by a majority of 29, and clause 10 to 26 were then gone through, being either carried, negatived, or postponed according to the intentions of the Govan meet.
THE BIRKBECK BUILDING SOCIETY.

The 42nd annual meeting of the Birkbeck Build- ing Society has been held at the Offices 29 and 30, Southaropton-buiktings, Chancery-lane. The report adopted states that the receipts during the year which ended 31st March last reached 42,169,030, making a total from the commsncement of the society of £163,297,213. The deposits received were £9,857,817, and the sulscriotions £215,871. The gross profits amounted to £213,867. The surplus funds stand at £5,727,331, of which £1,670,210 is invested in securities guaranteed by the British Government. Up- wards of £2,093,590 are registered in the books of the Bank of England. The cash in the hands of the bankers is £478,586. making £312,983 in excess of the liabilities. The subscriptions and deposits withdrawable on demand amount to £5,883,572. The surplus funds are sufficient to pay the depositors 114 per cent. on the amonat of their deposits. The new accounts opened during the year were 13.752, and there are altogether 67,244 share- holders and depositors on the books. Since its establishment, the society has returned to the shareholders and depositors £135,3.09,265, the whole amount having been re-paid upon demand. They have adopted the wise policy of investing a very large proportion of the deposits in Conssls etc., available at the shortest notice to meet any emergency that could arise in times of financial embarassment and distrust. ,No better proof of the soundness of this policy and the !strength of the Society's position could be afforded than ' that given by the manner in which it Met the run brought about in September last, by the collapse of the "Liberator " and its allied companies during which period £1,578,005 was withdrawn, and there was suffi- cient to have paid every Depositor in full. A large pro- portion of the money withdrawn was re-deposited,and, attracted by the evideace of stability thus afforo'ed, the number ormembers and depositors has largely increased.

div.head: Zettas to tin eittor.
div.p: Zettas to tin eittor.
A VARIATION ON "ASIERICAN NOTES."

Sir,—The reading of Mr. Whitham's very suggestive American Rotes, like other things from the same pen, affords one much material for reflection. First, as to the big-immensity of almighty dollar-land and its mighty spry inhabitants. Wall,now ! I calculate that must be one of Brother Jonathan's stretchers, when he claims for his lakes to contain one-half of all the fresh water of the globe! Quite right this if the word open were added. The globe has vast stores of fresh water underlying its Surfer*. But having enjoyed exceedingly a run thr-ugh these most magnificent lakes, I will riot repay the plea- Sure by running them down. Were I to do so I should feel reproached by my sunny memories of the Thousand Wands, of the beautiful Thunder Bay, and the rapid Sault St. Marie. And what an experience for a War- ringtonian, to be able to draw a bucket of water over the side and quench his thirst—to be able to go to sea without a store of water! Then, as to heresy-hunting. Quite characteristic of the land is this! Mr. Whitham says :—" The Presbyte- rians of the States seem to have a strong leaven of Cal- vinism in their composition." This is quite true ; and the cause is not far to seek. The descendants of the peasantry of Eurepe, they hold the religious opinions of the last or preceding centuries, overlaid, but slightly mitigated by a superficial polish. And then they are too much absorbed in dollar-piling to hive time to de- vote to that culture that might clear their minds from these deadening superstitions. And they pay their par- sons to keep them in this state of inherited dogma ; hoisting him from his office if he dare to attempt their enlightenment, as in the case menti,ned by Mr. Whit. ham.

_ Very noticeablo,too,is what I call the traces of the sea, er rather of the sea-transit of themselves or parents. I believe " chawing " with its most objectionable accom- paniment is one result of temporary contact with tarry Jack. Again, they do not harness a horse —they "hitch UP" and " go aboard " where we, more quietly, take our seats.

Politically and socially,America has many of the follies of extreme youth ; they are yet sowing their wild oats, and possibly the whirlwind has yet to be reaped. Poll- tically,l believe the States have a deterrent effect on the advance of Republican ideas in England, owing to the extravagance, and peculation, and vulgar Plutocracy prevailing over there. Recruited from the ranks of those who have " left their country for their coentry's good" little good can be expected of their interference in the politics of their adopted country. Meanwhile, we in Eng- land, thou,gli with eyes tired by the sycophancy of those who forget that it is possible te be loyal to the crown and disloyal to the people-- if we turn te our fickle neighbour— Prance—little better encouragement is found, for there indeed, we see grown up children playing at young Re- publicanism. But it yet remains for the staid concen- trativeness of England to show to the world the 21orious example of peaceful Republicanism—of a people truly self-ruling and self-respecting. This contingency, like the sword of Damocles, hangs o'er the head of royalty by the thread of good behavi.ur. In this way we are at present happily free,at once from ti* e horrors of Auto- cracy and the evils of a Republican scramble for place and power. Nevertheless, if some fine morning we awake and find that the whole of our royalty bad been, by the dispensa- tion of a merciful Providence, translated to the " Land of the leal,"—l am quite persuaded that the same Provi- dence would not be implored to re-instate them. As practical folk, we should acquiesce in the ruling of Pro- vidence, and try to make shift with the Premier for the time being, the man who at present rules over us but is ric)t called our ruler. .We would accept the reality, even if we lost the sham.-1 am, dm,
JOHN PEERS.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY.
A WARRINGTON FIREMAN FALLS OFF lIIS ENGINE.

Alexander Meldram, aged 26 years, employed as a fireman, on the London and North-Western Railway and residing at 28 Forster-st.. Warrington, died at the Infirmary, on Monday afternoon, from injuries received the same day on the railway. He had left Warrington by the 2-35 passenger train for Northwich in company with the engine driver Joseph Pennington, and from some reason he had fallen off the engine and was picked up in an uncon- scious state near Preston Brook statton,from whence he was immediately brought to Warrington by the 2-55 mail, and then c:nveyed to the Intirmacy on a stretcher, by railway inspector Peters and a porter named James Whittakar. He died an hour and a half after admittance to the Infirmary, and never recovered consciousness.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

Mr. S. Brighouse held the inquest upon the deceased on Wednesday afternoon, at the Infirmary. Mr. Fenna, solicitor, represented the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Mary Ann Meldrum, wife of the deceased identified the body. She last saw him alive at 1-15 on Monday afternoon, when he left home to go on duty. She did not see him again until the next morn- ing.—Joseph Pennington, the engine driver, said that he lived at 23 Alcard-st., Warrington. Deceased was acting as his fireman, on Monday last. They left Bank Quay, high level station, by the 2-35 passenger train far Northwich. That was deceased's first journey for the day, and he was quit:, sober at the time. The first stop was at Moore, and then at Preston Brook, between which stations the accident occurred. After the train left Moore it was cJstomary to send a jet of steam up the chimney of the engine, as the train had to stop at , Acton Bridge, to allow three express trains to pass, and the steam causes a draught up the chimney, and by this means there is no nuisance from smoke while stop- ping at Acton Bridge. On the present occasion wit- ness Was applying the jet, when he last saw deceased. , Deceased was then standing on the fireman's side of the engine, on the footplate inside the rail. They were jug entering the short tunnel about a hundred yards on the : Moore side .of Preston Brook station, and he 'Hissed deceased immediately afterwards. Witness drew up at Preston Brook station anel informed the station master and guard who then wimt to look for the deccased. Witness was obliged to go on with his train to Acton Bridge and did not see deceased again until that day.—ln answer to questions by the Coroner, witness said that the engine was a tank engine going tank first. It had no tender. The opening on each side of the en- gine was 18 inches and they had to get in and out sideways. There was a ledge at the opening. Deceased must have fallen out sideways. Witness ,could not account for the accident, unless it was caused by the back draught which takes place when going under tunnels and causes flames to come out of the door. Deceased may have jumped backwards to escape the flame and thus have fallen out. Witness's clothes were singed at the same time that deceased fell out. Deceased had been with him four times previously. He wa4 a transfer man from Workington. Witness and deceased were on good terms. Witness had never heard of a man falling from the inside of an engine before.—Hr. Bowden, house surgeon at the infirmary, said deceased was admitted into the infirmary on Monday at 3.30 p.m. He wag dying and died at five o'clock. He did not appear to have been run ovgr. He was bleeding from wounds on the scalp, nose, mouth, and ears, and there were bruises on other parts of the body. His clothing smelled of burning. He was unconscious to the time of his deatli.—William Sherwood, the guard of the trim, said the driver told tarn of the accident at Pr, i Brook station and lie went in company with William Taylor, the station- master, to look for deceased. They found him lying. unconscious, face downwards outside the four foot, just outside the tunnel near the station. Witness, who is an ambulance man gave first aid, and an express train to Warrington was stopped and Mr. Taylor took charge of him to Warrington. When found, deceased's clothes were smoaldering. Witness had to go on with his train as soon as he SAW deceased put into the express.—Mr. .Sudlow, a juryman, thought something should he done, ! if possible to obviate the danger arising from the back draught from the fire, as otherwise there might be other i accidents arising from the same cause in the future.— William Preston Brook stationmaster, corrobor- ated the guard's evidence and said that lie took deceased , to Warrington. A hospital nurse, who was in the I .express, also gave every assistance in her power.—By Mr. Fenna : Everything was done that could be done for deceasod.—Bartholemew Marshall, locomotive fore- mayl, Warrington, said that he had been foreman for the Land N.-W. Co. for ten years, and understood the con- struction of engines well. The cab of the engine was 41t. 6in. by alfc. 2in., and the hand rail was four feet hi,h. He thought that the driver's suggestion was the tu7ist likely thing to account for the accident, but he had never heard of a man falling out of an engine before.— The Coroner : Is it possible to make the door so as to prevent the hack draught ? Witness : No it is not. Everything is done that can be done, but the draught is too strong. There is no remedy.—The Coroner in sum- ming up said that it was a matter entirely for the jury, as there Was no law for him to explain. Thy back draught was a risk to which engine drivers and firemen were expoced, and they had to submit to it as part of their duty, as there was no remedy for it at present. Although it was distressing to think that men ran this risk,it could not be avoided. There was therefore no law that could be enforced in the present case. —After a short deliberation the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental Death."
