CRICKAT.

I will never prophecy any more—unless I can speak with positive certainty. I confidently assured all my friends, and other people's friends, that Warrington first eleven were going to come out with flying colours in their match with Sale on Saturday. And sure enough no one can deny that that aley had come out with flying colours,—but they lost the game, just the same.

Sale only won by 13 runs-132 to 119; and it is not likely they would have managed this had it not been for a little oversight upon the part of thc captain. Voisey had to leave early to catch a train, and S. M. Crosfield forget to remove his name from the end of the batting list. Consequently Voisey had to leave without going in for his innings, and it is fair to surmise that had he not gone without his innings he would have stayed for them—no, I don't mean that, I mean it is fair to suppose he would most likely have , scored the 13 which Warrington required to avert de- feat. The game itself was a very funny one—there was sornething,about it all through that made you seem as if : you'd like to laugh, when your mouth had stopped smil- ing, just as you feel when you tickle your hand with a feather. Firstly, the remarkable manner in which the scores of the two teams tapered down, was AR eloquent appeal to any remote mustard seed of risibility that a man's bosom contained. Sale started with a 38, and a 40 and an 18 and then it all col- lapsed and shrunk up, and nobody else in the team seemed to trouble about making more than a 1 or, maybe, a 0. Warrington were just the same; they seemed as if they weren't going to be beaten, even in erratic scoring. S. M. Crosfield lead off with 40, Griffin followed with 29, and Sugg with 25 and then crash it all went into a shaky line of one's and duck's eggs—which one man in this case insinuated were geese eggs: and I thought it was uncalled for. People can't always play well.

There was another thing that made you want to laugh —or cry, played for Sale and wore a striped, bril- liantly coloured jacket, composed of such commingling hues of blinding, dazzling tints that the wearer at once became conspicious. At first he was mistaken fin a rainbow. But aft,rwards it was found be had been mistaken for a cricketer—a certain well known batsman. He seemed to take a huge delight in letting the ball run beneath his legs or drop between his fingers, when he was fielding. This made him a favourite with the spectators, and once, when he caught a hall—evidently a mistake—the whole field burst into a cheer, and the man with the coat of many colours lifted up his voice and shouted : "They don't seem to be used to cricket here" Many people are anxious to know who this humorous cricketer was.

Certain little chances, that I think are wise, are likely to be carried out in the arranging of the first eleven. For instance I believe the captain is going to bring Bibby forward from the 2nd eleven into the front ranks. This is good. Bibby has played a very high-class game with his eleven this season, and he certainly deserves promo- tion. This is not an invidious selection from his team; no reflection upon the other players, they are all good players; indeed they all deserve promotion—but Bibby most. Now that will show I am not prejudiced. Certain other players in the first eleven are likely to be " dropped out,' too. Then again I was very pleased to, that W. Podmore was put upon the bowling again. He did not have any particularly good luck with his bowling, except to stop the scoring, but still we all know that those peculiar slow balls of his are worth bringing forward a little more.

R. Smith was away again on Saturday, and he is becoming such a regular absentee from the IS arrington matches now, that I am afraid he'll slip right over :nto the county second entirely, if he is not secured a little ruore firmly here. Well, let honour be to whom .honour belongs. Mr. R. Smith deserves county honours and if he gets them let us first congratulate him, and then console the Warrington team afterwards.
Warrington second and Site second pretty well made a draw of the game. For eleven wickets Sale made 11 and for ten wickets Warrington scored 111. Hamps on made the top s':ore for Warrington by 23.

There was more inferior scf,ring among the junior teams of the locality on Saturday, than ever I remem- ber occurring before. Wycliffe Juniors met Trinity. They kad four duck's and the highest score was 10, whilst Trinity had seven ducks, with the highest score at four ! We get to Buckley-street and Bewsey-road Wesleyans. and find the former with -seven ducks and the latter with six. Further on we arrive at the Co- operative Stores and Orford Barracks. The latter we find with nine ducks. I can understand a preference for ducks accompanied with green peas, but such a universal_preference for the " ducks " in cricket shows simply enough the Warrington juniors are a poor ht of players.

Sankey Wire Mills seems to be the only team with its head over water, now. They met Crewe Trinity Wes- leyans on Saturday and scored 95 against 25. And the scoring was even, too, which shows that the mill men are going in—if you will excuse the expression—are going in to mill men who have thought themselves of better calibre. lam glad of this. A week or two ago I was discouraged with them ; but hope has been re- kindled, and doubt been put at rest. That is a sent- ence worth patenting. Ihrshall shnwei up well again in howling. He took five wickets for ten runs, and he made the second best score in batting.

The Warrington first eleven always look upon their visit to Liverpool as a pleasant one. They went to Liverpool on Thursday afternorm,after spending a morn- ing in anxious apprehension of seeing an extra dose of tear drops fall from old Man Pluvious up aloft. But old Sal turned out and smiled a bit instead—and so did the cricketers. The match was a very tight one, and may well be called a draw. Liverpool for all wickets made 155, whilst Warrington for 10 wickets made 144. G. Clarke came out of his shell—as it were—and made a fair score; it amounted to 49. Voisey also made 23. J. J. Crosfield and G. Clarke did all the bowling, taking the whole of the wickets. •

It is my painful duty to announce that the Wye Val- ley tourists have arrived back alive. No, that doesn't sound right. It is my pain—oh !Itis my pleaxing duty— that is better. How these words do mix up as if they were twins. Yes, they have got back. There were six of them, Messrs. D. Davies, J. Podmore, T. Davies, Whittle, C. Welsh, W. Lesley. They were under the control of the chaplain. They travelled altogether 450 miles, and consider they had one of the most enjoyable tours that it is possible to have in the country, and they were favoured with fine sunny weather, all the while. It was too sunny, and they ought to have had proper head protectors for one of them told me that once the sun beat down upon them so powerfully that it com- menced to frizzle the hair of one of the party. The wonder is he did not get a sunstroke.

- There was one peculiar adventure which herel the tourists. Three of them at the conclusion of thr third day discovered that they had worn oat tho seats of their riding pants, and ccrisequently they- had to have an hours rest in bed whilst patches were not stitched on, but insulated.

div.head: BASEBALL.
div.p: BASEBALL.

Base hal is a very interesting game, hut seems to be two quiet for people who live in the midst of the thrilling perfarmances given by exponents of football. We have a base trdl club in Warri neon. but I do not hear much of it. While almost all other games have been takiag rest this week, this particular club has been putting in another appearance. It met the Eden Hill club on Satur- day. and lost by 13 points. The game, however, was a very good one, and also a very pleasant one, its conclu- sion being foll3wed by a tea in which both teams joined.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.

How sorry I feel for the members of the Warrington Association?Anglinir For two years they have been first struggling for possession of, and then stocking, the fish- ing length at Walton Arch's. Only last week the length was opened for the firAt time, and last Wednes- day the whole of the fish were sent to " pot "—not the boiling one, hot the figurative one. A culvert connect- ing the length with the canal burst and flooded the fish- ing water so that it inundated the basks, and carried all the fish into the neighbouring brooks and ditches. There has been close upon £4O worth of fish lost besides much damage being done to the length.

One remarkable thing is that the towing path running along the length has been broken away to the extent of nine feet Inland. It is most difficult to concEiye how a flush of water could do this, and it is suspected by some members of the club that there has been explosion at work.

div.head: TRAFFIC IN OLD HORSES.
div.p: THE TRAFFIC IN OLD HORSES.
WARRINGTON APPEAL CASE: A DEFEND- ANT'S DISAPPEARANCE.

Some time ago, a Belgian, named Edward Collins appealed against a sentence of three months' imprisonment, passed upon him by the Warrington magistrates, for causing two horses to be travelled from Chester to Manchester, afterwards intending to take them to Grimsby and then for shipment to Antwerp. The animals were sworn to be totally 1 wilit for the journey. and Collins was accordingly sentenced to three months' imprisontnent, and his agent John Atherton received two weeks' hard labour. Mr. Florner. solicitor. or Liverpool, the following week applied for Collins' release on bail, pending the hearing. of the case at the Liverpool Sessions. Ball of £4O was granted, and the case was fixed to be heard at the Liverpool sessions on Mon- day, but as neither the defendant nor his counsel turned up, the bail was estreated, and an order was made ouc for the delinquent's commitment.
TEE REV. JOSEPH ELLISON INTER- VIEWED.
AN INTERESTING CONVERSATION.

An " Examiner " reporter the other day went down to Latchford, to have a chat with the Rev.. Joseph Ellison, who is sojourning there during a short vacation there from the States. In the course of the conversation the reporter said : " Did you go abroad for the purpose of joining the ministry,Mr. Ellison ? " "Oh, no ! My object really in going to America ! was to take up a journalistic life. I arrived in Bos- ton in April, 1892, in company with Mr. John S Green, who was taking a tour over there. Through the kindness of a Mr. Carpenter, an editor of one of the Boston papers, I became a privileged mem- ber of the Press Club in the city,and each day used to write applications from there for journalistic appointments. In a few days I received a letter from one of the papers in Worcester MEM% asking me to join their staff at once. I did sp.'' "And how did you like newspaper work ? " " Well," resumed Mr. Ellison with a smile. "I soon tired of journalism—at least the class of journ- alism I was called upon to perform. Being the junior member of the staff—not by age, bat by rotation—my assignments, or engagements, were of a very unsavoury kind. The work indeed lost its charm to me—there was no real objsct or purpose to attain, and so my interest dwindled all away in three weeks," and Mr. Ellison laughed in remembrance of the time. " Yes, in three weeks' time I left the press and tool: an appoint- ! merit in an office. And this is where the serious part of my story commences. Very naturally, hav- ing lost my interest in journalism, having seen some of my cherished hopes wither away,and being fallen upon the humdrum work of a clerk again, I began to feel discouraged at heart. Now,l had from the first attached myself to to the Baptist Church, in Worcester, and one day whilst attending a meet- . _ .

_ ing of the congregation we learned that the pastor's wife had been taken seriously ill. A day or two afterwards I met the pastor in the street and expressed my sorrow at hearing of his wife's illness. He turned to me very abruptly—he is a very abrupt little gentleman —and said: "My wife is dead, Mr. Ellison." I was naturally distressed, and when about to leave him,' expressed my regret that I did not know his con- gregation better, or I would gladly have preached for him on Sunday. He seemed very much sur- prised, and said : " Why, you are the very kind of man we have been baking for. We want someone like you to fill the pulpit at our Greendale Chapel." Well, the result of this was that I preached on the Sunday for the pastor, much to the surprise of the congregation. Then the following week the pastor asked me to preach in his pulpit in the morning and he would be present, and then go to Greendale in the evening and preach there. 1 did this, with the result that I was asked to take charge of the Greendale Church for three months. This revived my hopes, and stimulated me to work again, and during those three months I worked steadily along at my office in the daytime and at the church in the evenings. The conclu- sion of the three months began to get near, and then there commenced some talk about asking me to take the pastorship of Greendale ; and indeed I was asked and consented to undergo a theological examination before an assembly of ministers of the locality and Doctors of Divinity. The examination was a very strict one,and although I passed through the ordeal successfully, it was with a considerable amount of apprehention. But I got through—to use an Americanism--and am delighted with my congregation." " Is the system of service and work there similar to that in England." "I.So, not exactly. The people only have two meals, Sundays, there, an ordinary service is held at 10.30, which continues to 12, then at 12.30 there

is Sunday School Session. In this almost the whole mgregation join —elders and oungsters—and the session continues until about two, alter which the people go to a late dinner." " Are the Sunday Schools conducted as they are here?'

_ "Oh, no ! After a general introductory service has taken place, the various classes go to their respective class-rooms, and here you may see any Sunday, a feature of Sunday School work entirely different from anything in England. A subject is chosen by the teacher for instruction. The scholars are made acquainted with the subject, and then they debate upon it—no matter what the subject is, an unrestricted debate, so it be rational, is allowed." - -
" In English schools there would be an objection to allowing open debates, especially to sceptics or atheists."

"Not so there. The classes are entirely educa- tional, and the American church-going people are thoroughly acquainted with the Bible, are ever ready to thrash out a theological point. Why not long before I left the States, the Rev. Mr. Butler and Mr. Whitham attended our Sunday School, and had a regular set to, in debate. The subject was prayer, and Mr. Whitham denied the efficacy of prayer, whilst Mr. Butler supported it. Then there is another thing. No business connected with the Sunday School is allowed to accumulate. It is tran- sacted each Sunday as ic occurs."
The evening service—is there anything differ- ent in that ?"

"Yes. It is different to the English evening service. ID the dist place the congregations in America do not care much for ser- mons in the evening and the service commonly is turned into a service of song, or perhaps a child- ren's concert, with a religious element in it, or it might be an illustrated lelture. Then the Church business like the Sunday school business, is not allowed to accemmulate. Each Thursday there is a covenant meeting, or prayer meeting, and all business that may be on hand is transacted hero. Then another new feature presents itself. The pas- tor usually speaks for a short time, after which the congregation discuss the various points in the address, and these discussions are quite commonly taken part in by lady mem- bers of the congregation. The Americans are somewhat puritanical in their interpretation of the Bible. They believe very greatly in annihilation, and they will bring up all the phrases in the Old Testament in which there is any figurative mention of the sinner being burned up, and a common one is, "The wages of sin is death," which many of them assert simply means annihilation. So I find it an interesting task to debate these subjects." "You say the people are somewhat Puritanical— do you mean generally so?" "Oh, dear, no! Merely upon the subject of anni- hilation; it seems to be one of the legacies left by the old Puritan settlers. In ordinary life they appear more genial than the English people; indeed I may say many of them are rather flippant. And, perhaps I might say that there is a difference be- tween the American and English children of a rather marked character, for the American children seem to he brought up with no regard or honour for what are, in England, at least, reverenced. This may be attributable to their education for it is all undenominational, and fres there." " I presume —upon the rumours that reach us over here—that preaching in America is carried out on sensational lines."

" Well," said Mr. Ellison, " One cannot say on sensational lines. Certainly if a preacher is able to bring home a truth by resorting to original expres- sion he does so. BM the formal style of preaching as practised here, is not reccgnised there. For in- stance we do not preach from a pulpit. There is a p:attorm with a reading desk upon ft, and if the minister wishes to read his sermon be can do FO from the desk, but if he cultivates a dramatic de- livery he may have the whole platform to walk about on. There is one preacher not far from Green- dale, who preaches to his congregation, always at- ' tired in a full dress suit."
"Well now,in social life are the people considered to be more moral than here ?"

"I think so. In the first place you do not see one fourth the drunkenness that one may see here. We have local option there, you know,but the decisions for a local majority only holds good for 12 months. For instance in Greendale, at the last election but one, the drinking saloons were closed, but at the last election one was opened. The licenses, how- ever. are extremely heavy." " How is drunkenness dealt with by the police there."

"in an enti-ely different style to the English one They do not, watt until a man is incapable or dis- orderly there. If he appears in the street, intoxic- ated he is taken into custody. There are poles all about the city on which are boxes with electric communications both with the police and the fire :tations. The policeman i•imply touches a button, and presently the patrol will appear and take away the prisoner. The next. morning he 6 tried. If it be his first offence, or even his second, he is dis- charged with a caution,and his name is not allowed to appear in the paper. But after the second offence be is dealt severely with ; fines are not

div.p: FIHF IPX AVNER T I D A 11, J t - lO, 18(X3. I A.,* • 7. 1

inflicted,it is .it her wfort rigbes or a month's incar- ceration. But speaking of tl electric poles letninds me of the lire alarms. Their! is one of these poles in every blreet, conneeted with a local hose at ation. The poles are numbered, awl immediately the alarm ,is given the tire engine witheut any delay come ! right down to the street where the fire is At the . same time there is a general alarm raised all over the city. The communications extend to all the buzzes, or whistles at the large works. According to the number of the 1-nles these alarms throw out a signal of location. For instance if the number of the pole is 32 the buzzes will emit three succes- sive sounds, then follows a short pause, and then two more sounds, to represent 32. People at once get to know the locality, and when the fire is out the alarms give one wave pf whistle and buzz, an 1 the people know the fire is out.

div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

MISTAKIN6I CORPSES. A GRIM DISCUSSION. The fortnightly meeting of the IVarrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday. Mr. 0. Ratcliffe presided, and there were also present :—The Rev. G. F. Roberts, Dr. Pattison, and Messrs. R. Ileaton, Gill, W. Houghton, J Houghton, A. J. Jolley, Shaw, Muir, Aukland, Hill, Balharry, Clarke, Longton, Smith, Turton, Hub- bert, Pilling, Warburton, and Fairclough.

div.head: BURIED THE WHOICO NAN.
div.p: BURIED THE WHOICO NAN.

Dr. Farrisms said he wished to know *what the exist- ing arrangements were in the way of communicating with the friend:4 of any person whodied in their hospital. He had been informed by a woman named Broom of Newton, that her husband had died in their hospital on the last Friday in June. She was not made aware of this until the following Tuesday when she received the following telegram : "Jelin died—funeral to-y. Wire instructions if any, before noon." She wired to the effect that she would bury her deceased husband at Newton, and was about to come over to Warrington when she received another message to the effect that "he was buried yesterday." He believed the woman had been very much distressed about this and he asked for some explanation. There had evidently been some serious mistake.

The CLEM'S explained that Mr. Ward, the master, who was away no his holidays was going to draw up a report upon the matter, a hich he had no doubt would be a perfectly satisfactory one. Mr. flineenT : The deceased man's relatives have in- formed me that two of the nephews visited the man Broom the week before he died, and left their aunt's address for communication, in case anything happened. Flie CLeas said he did not think it was fair to the Master to discuss the matter before he, submitted his re- port, which he had agreed to prepare a 4 the last meeting of the House Committee, just before he went on his holidays. From what he (the Clerk) could understand, it seemed that three inmates, including Broom, all died on the same day and were consequently measured for their coffins. It was inconvenient to bury more , than two at once, and so Mr. Ward had given instruc- tions that on Monday two of the corpses—not including Broom—should be interred on Monday. By some mis- take Broom's coffin was brought on Monday,and Broom was buried that day. Mr. Ward, however, was not aware of this, and under ordinary circumstances there would have been nothing whatever in it. On Tuesday morning. however, Mr. Ward got a letter from Mrs. Broom asking after her husband's health, and Mr. Ward despatched the telegram read by Dr. Pattison,but : learned afterwards that Broom had been interred by mistake. Mr. Ward was in no way to blame in this, for he would most certainly have written to the widow, at the time of death had he known her address then. " "

Mr. Ilimsear : But how could he have telegraphed to her it he did not know her address,? Tile CLERK : lie did not know her address until he received a letter Irom her on Tuesday. Mr. GILL : It seems to be a strange thing that the address of the relatives of an inmate should not be known.
Tile CLERK : In this case Broom, is a man who was removed from the Prestwich Asylum here, and he was never visited by Ida friends or relatives, so no one knew who he helonxed to.

Mr. IlEaTo-N saidv he thought the matter was clear enough, and there was no blame to be attached to tn., master of the House. Indeed he could safely say that all the officials were anxious to give ttici friends of any inmate full facilities to bury him in a case of death. kflear, hear.)

Mr. LoNiTrox : Well, the matter is a very grave one, and Mr. Ward should report upon it. 'the CHAIRMAN' : The deceased person never contri- buted flue penny towards his maintenance, neither did his friends.

Mr. HINUERT : That does not matter, sir. His wife had every right to see him before he was buried, and bad every right to bury him at her own expense. Tile CHAIRMAN : 01 course. I didn't mean to dis- pute that. Upon Dr. Pattison expressing himself satisfied with the explanation the matter was dropped, until the Master's report should be received. -- - - LEGAL EXPENSES.

Mr. B. SHEARER, relieving o-tlic7r-,.next submitted his quarterly accounts. They contained art item of £8 as legal expenses for the recovery of sums due to the Union on orders of maintenance passed be the magistrates. The total amount was £22o.—Mr. William Houghton thought the item for legal expenses was very hos vy,and he could not tmderstand it.—Mr. Shearer then explained that in consequence of constant proceeding having to be taken against the persons on whom the orders were made, legal expenses and incidental expenses had to be incurred. On one occasion he had been compelled to follow a mail to Loti‘lon, and ho very often had to leave town after them. Unless they kept up a vigorous grip upon these peciele the maglstratrs' orders would he dis- reaarded with contempt.—Mr. Longtm agreed that Mt Shearer's explanation was satisfactirry. It was mon. necessary for them, as a duty to the ratepayers, to keep a strict hand upon those on whom orders were made, than it was to make the collection of the orders a com- mercial succi-iss. (Bear, hear.) The matter then dropped.

DIDN'T KNOW HOW AM GOT THERE. Mr. Wm. BouottroN drew attention to the fact that last .IhurBdav he come down to the house to see the treat to the inmates, when he was asked to join in the meeting of the House Committee. He was not aware that he was a member of the committee. Ho knew he de• chimed the offer of a seat on the committee, and he didn't know how he got there. It must have been a mistake on the part of the Clerk, he thought.—The CLERIC thought not, and as the Board seemed to think with the Clerk—er that they had gut a good man on the commit- tee—they pleasantly persuaded Mr. Houghton not to have his name expunged from the committee.

div.head: TIIE ROYAL WEDDING.
div.p: TIIE ROYAL WEDDING.
LETTER FROM TETE QUEEN.

Her Majesty the Queen has addressed a letter to the people ot the Empire. The Queen expresses to the people bow deeply gratified an touched she has been by the "loyalty and devotion" evinced on the occasion of the wedding of her grandson, the Duke of York, to the Princess Victoria Mary. Her Majesty adds that in weal or woe she has ever met with the warmest and kindest sympathy, and that she knows that the people of this vast Empire are aware how truly her heart beats for them in all their joys and sorrows. t' In the existence of this tie between the people and herself lies the real strength of the Empire."

I bear writes a London correspondent, from Wolferton that the Duke and Duchess of York are frequentiy seen out there on driving tburs,Princess May generally hand- ling the pAr of ponies attached to a low phaeton. The bride and bridegroom appear extremely happy togethr but although Bachelor's Cottage, now re-named York Cottage, is away from the busy whirl of life, they are inundated with telegrams and letters from all parts of the country wishing them joy. The cottage is so small that the Duke of York's household has been put up in temporary buildings close at hand, and even Lady Eva Neville, Prineess May's lady-in-waiting, has also been lodged outside the building. On Thursday the bride and bridev,ruom make their first public appearance since the wedding, at the shorthorn sale at Sandringham, where they will meet all the members of the Prince of Wales's family. After another week they are to return to town and go to a seasKle place for a fortnight, eventually findiro, themselves in the first week in August in Cowes, for the Royal Yacht Squadron week.

div.head: PROPOSED OCK-OUT OF SHOEMAKERS.
div.p: PROPOSED OCK-OUT OF SHOEMAKERS.

A Northampton correspondent statPs that the shoe manufacturers have at a meeting of their Federation decided on a general Jock-out, to commence on Monday, July 21th. This step has been taken on account of'the action of the operatives' union with reference to the disputes now existing at Bristol and Birmingham.
THE REPRESENTATION OF TAUNTON.

RESIGNATION OF THE HON. A. P. ALLSOPP. It is announced ti at the Hon. Alfred Percy Allsopp s has resigned his seat as Conservative member for the boroughh e succeeded Taunton. He has held hi seat since 1887, n eceeded Ids brother, Lord ilindlip, on the e latter's elevation to the peerage. At the last election the Conservative majority was 431.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.

A VISIT TO THE SHIP CANAL WORKS. We extract the following from anntrticle on the Ship Candi Works in the" Manchester Weekly Times." "It is hardly likely that the Warrington Docks, estimated to involve a cost of over £lOO,OOO will, as officially notitied to Mr.J.Lyon Whittle, the Town Clerk, be conspleted by the end of the present year. Those docks will have a ' water space of 221 acres, or about one third less than ' that of the Manchester Docks; the length of the quays will he •two-thirds of a mile, and their area equal to seven acres. Approaching Warrington, we are entering upon historic ground, for we are now at Wilderspool, the Roman Veratinurn, where, on the elevated ground op- posite the Arplay meadows, and between the river and Stockton Heath, the subjects of the Cassars established a camp to safeguard the passage of the Mersey at Wilders- pool Causeway. It was an important position, for here the great military way from Chester tattle North, which proceeded by way of Hoots Bank, and beneath the oamp on Heishy Hill and Frodsharn, was joined by another road from Condate the present Kinderton ad- joining Middlewich, and which, crossing the river, en- tered Lancashire by way of Mersey-street and Fennel- street, in Warrington. During the cutting of the Old Quay Canal in 1801-3, numerous foundations of Roman buildings.together with bases, shafts, and capitals of columns, were found at a distance of above seven feet below the surface, affording the clearest evidence of Noman occupation, and at different times subsequently coins, pottery, vases, lamps, fibulae. Bm. have been turned up,- many examples of which 'have been deposited in the Warrington Museum. During the Civil Wars Stockton Heath was the scene of a sharp military encounter. The people of Warrington, taking tone from the powerful Stanley, took sides with the King.„and fenced the town about with mud walls,whenc.o the Iforaliat troops occasionally made predatory incur- sions into the surrounding country, making free, where. ever they had an opportunity with the property of their opponents. This was more than the Parliamentarians could tolerate, and at last they resolved that an effort should be made to dislodoe them. " Upon Monday in Easter Week (April 3, 1643)," says Burghall, the Puritan author of "Providence Improved," "Captain Ardern and some other captains with their companyes, cYid face the town (Warrington); but the Earle, perceaving their strength but small (for neither Coll. Brereton nor Man- chaster forces were yet come up to them), issued forth with great strength into Cheshire side, where the Parlia- ment soldiers were, slew some, took other prisoners.and tied like to have routed them all, had not Coll. Brereton, with his forces came at the instint to their assistance, which the Earle perceaving, being then on Stockton Heath, where the skirmish was, retired speedily into the town, having lost some of his men." Stockton Heath is now the scene of less exciting; inci- dents. Where the broad heathy waste stretched in wild and untitled solitude, traversed only by the rough and rutty road that !ed from Northwich by way ot Bud- worth and Stretton to Wilderspool, a pleasant hamlet has sprung up ;. thanks to the liberality of Messrs. Green all, a pretty Gothic church, dedicated to St Thomas, with a neatly laid out God's acre surrounding it, was erected some 50 Sr 60 years ago, which forms a pretty feature on ths landscape. Afterwards the accom- paniments of a parsonage house and a parochial school were added, and the place has since been constituted a separate parish. The excavation for the canal runs juot below the church, and where the road along which Colonel Brereton and his Puritan troopers marched from Northwich„ crosses the line, some heavy engineering work has to be carried out. The Latchford Canal, which had a junction with the Mersey here, had to be stopped, and it has been decided to construct a barge lock connecting it with the canal; in this con- siderable progress has been made. What has been knowt. as the Twenty-step Bridge over the old canal is about to be removed. The North wich-road has been a great obstacle to the completion of the canal at this point, and a swing bridge of ponderous dimensions has had to be constructed a little to the eastward of it. This bridge is practically completed, and the approaches are in a very forward state. As soon as they are ready and the bridge opened for traffic, the roil will be diverted. The removal of the old road will then be immediately commenced, and the channel for the canal cut through. One advantage will be that the new road here will have a somewhat straight- er line than its predecessor. though it will make havoc with some of the dwelling-house property in tho imp& diate locality, for, while at present the road runs in front of a row of houses, the diversion will run close by the backs of them, rejaining the old road nearly oppo- site Messrs. Greenall's brewery. Some distance beyond the North wich-road bridge on the right an opening has been constructed to give entrance from the canal to the new Warrington docks, and a little further on the line is crossed by a traffic Swing bridge, known as the Stag Inn Bridge, and here a new road is being constructed, and is now nearly finished, which will connect the bridge wth River-st., Warrington. From this point to where the canal is crossed by the London and North-Western Grand Junction Railway, and_ the joint lines of the lirkenhearl, Lancashire, and Cheshire Junction .Ratl-
I Ora

'ay, the excavations are virtually completed, and the new deviation lines, which have been ready and in work log order for some time, form a prominent feature in the distance. They are of course carried at.,a much higher level than the old lines, and we may add, as is the case at Latchford and at Irlam, they are very fine examples of engineering skill." THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY • - AND THE DEVIATIONS. - The deviations caused by the Ship Canal works at Welton, and Latchford, on the London and North- Western Railway, were used for the first time for pass- enger traffic on Sunday evening. The lines have since the first of March f,been used for goods traffic, and also officially tested. The first passenger train over the Latchford deviation was the 8-15 train to Liverpool -om Manchester, on Sunday night, and the 11-32 p.m. 'n from Chester was the first ovor the Arpley route. a was last week a very quiet part of the ship canal :orks at Latchford, has now become the busiest part of ..he section.. No fewer than six steam navvieEt, and about 300 navvies have been at work there duririaie week. The old railway is now being pulled up, and where the old line crosses the canal, the steam navvies working at each end have now almost met. The swing bridge near to, is being paved with wooden blocks, and is now almost cbmpleted. The new rails.; sy station, which is now in daily use is a great improvement on ti% old one. That dangerous practice of crossing and re- crossing the line, which was necessary at the old station in order to get a ticket, and on entering and leavingjba, platform, is now done away with. The tickets are now prrcured on entering the station, and a subway is pro- vided for reaching the opposite platform. It is confidently believed by those best able to judge that the Ship Canal works from Eastham to Warrington will he completed within two months, and that the canal will hoop:nett in accordance with previous state- ments early in 1894.

DESTROYING INSULATORS. The telegraph service between Manchester and Lymm was interfered with on Sunday/owing to the destruction of insulators by boys In the neighbourhood of Manchester. No fewer than 50 insulators were broken in one day, but, fortunately, two boys were apprehended and were brouelt before Mr. Leresehe at the County Police Court, Manchester. on Monday, and severely reprimanded. . DEATH OF MRS. THOMASON.—Mrs. ' Tholcason; relict of the late Mr. Thomason, who for many years was a member of the Local Board and the Board of Guardians died on Wednesday at the age of 73. The funeral took place on Saturday. Service for the dead was first read by the Rev. G. H. Southall, in the Primitive Methodift chapel, of which denomination the deceased had been an active member. The funeral cortege then proceeded to the Lyrnm Churchyard, where the deceased was in- terred in the presence of a large and sympathetic as- sembly of spectators. The Rev. E. T. Mills, Stockport, read the prayers over the grave.

div.p: rENKETH.

SEYana -vVaaittEtt.—Thunderstertns of an exceedingly severe nature have been prevalent in this distrait during last week. The rain has been very heavy, but as far has not done any damage to th 3 corn. RESCUE FROM DROWNING.—Last week a young man from this village, William Jackson. was bathing in the lake at:..outtiport with two friends, when one of them got into very deep water, and being a very indifferent swimmer lost his presence of mind and went under. His two companions were sum,- distance away but swam tip, and with great difficulty and no little personal risk suc- ceeded in getting him to the shore. He was quite in- sensible, and Jackson, who has attended the ambulance lectures in the village, proceeded to render first aid,and after about twenty minutes his efforts were rewarded. The members of the ambulance class are pleased that their work should have been of use so soon. Several minor Cases have been met with since the formation of the class, and been successfully treated.

div.head: PRESCOT WATCH FA CTO It T.
div.p: PRESCOT WATCH FA CTO It T.

On Thursday afternoon some sixty members of the Society of Chemical Industry, headed by Mr. Alfred Smetham, of Liverpool, travelled by special train from Lime-street Station to Prescot, to inspect the extensive works of the Lancashire Watchmaking Company. They were met at the works by Messrs. T. P. Ifiiwitt manag- ing director), Mr. James Hewitt (secretary), C. J. Hewitt, and W. L. Hindler, who conducted the party through the building. After inspecting the machine de Pertinent, the company WAS take* through the tool and press room, the frame, barrel, pinion, escape, flat, steel, jewelling, examining, time, dial, gilding, and finishing departments. The utmost interest was evinced by the visitors in the wonderful mechanism of the delicate machinery used in manufacturing the watch in its separate parts. The inspection war so well ordered that they first saw the making of the requisite tools, then the crude material from which the watches were made, and afterwards the various stages of manufacture up to the completed article. The party returned to Liverpool by special train, having spent an interesting and profitable two hours in seeing one branch of British industry which it is hoped has a bright future before it.

Alderman Sadler proposed the adoption el this Com- mittee's minutes. Councitior Christie seconded their adoption. The minutes contained the following items : —Lowerhouse Lane Sewer : Messrs. Sayce and Randle are proceeding slowly with this sewer. Ots the 16th inst., I found that they had laid the sewer invert blocks on rubbish instead of concrete for a distance 'Jf about 12 yards, which I had taken up, and cautioned tkie Clerk of Works to watch more carefully. Certificate. has been I made out for £330. Main and Secondary Roads: The Lancashire County Council have paid the sums agreed up- on for the maintenance and repairs of the above roads : Main roads £358, secondary roads £112; totai, £470. Councillor Rullough asked if the correspondence which had taken place between the Corporation and Messrs. Save' and Randle, might be read. This was agreed to and the Town Clerk read a letter sent to the firm from the Surveyor. The Surveyor stated that lie had been watching the work and seen the men laying the sewer blocks on rubbish instead of concrete, fie described this as '4 scamping work," and as the Clerk of the Works was on the spot at the time, he thought the matter was all the more serious. Messrs. Sayce and Randle replied that they had been compelled to do this, as they could not obtain concrete then, but they thought it was the duty of the Surveyor :to have called their Clerk of the Works ageution to what did not give- him satisfaction. —The minutes were adopted.

div.head: HEALTH COMUITTRIL
div.p: HEALTH COMUITTRIL

Upon the motion of Councillor Neil,seconded by Coun- cillor Carney,the minutes of.this Committee were adopted The minutes contained the following repott ef the Medi- cal Officer of Health :—The following report of the Medical Officer of Health submitted and read. Births, 111 equal to 44.4 per 1,000; deaths (total), including 76 eq,ual to 30.4 per 1,000 ; children under 1 year, 351 equal to ioa per 1,000 ; children between 1 and 5 years I 10 equal to 4,0 per 1,000. The death rate is unusually' high this month ; but if, as on other occasions, you will notice the mortality among children under five years of age, which amounts to 45, and if this were subtracted from the total it would leave the rate of mortality of persons over five years of age comparatively small, namely,l2.4. per thousand. In consequence of the neg- lect of owners to put insanitary property into repair In Victoria-st., George-st., Edmund-st., and Brown-street,. Moss Bank, after repeated admonitions and notices, it was found necessary to summon them to appear before the magistrates, who ordered them to put the property into repair. We hope this may De a salutary warning to others under shnilartonditiens. In company with the Sanitary Inspector, I visited several cowsheds within the-jurisdiction of the Corporation, and found in many instances they did not comply with the regulations. Others were of a model character and deserve high com- mendation. The last case of smallpox notified, from 24, Miltort-road,,being the husband of a woman now lathe hospital, and convalescent, is of a very mild type, and the case was removed to the hospital without delay. There is no trace of any other case in the Borough and we hope we have succeeded in stamping it out."—The Nuisance Inspector's report contained the following Six patients have been removed to the Infectious Diseases Hospitil, consisting of 3 typhoid, 2 smallpox, and erysipelas. The disinfecting ot the clothing, bedding arid premises has been duly attended to. In each case the premises were found clean.

div.head: GAS AND WATED COMMITTEE .-NSW ENGINE..
div.p: GAS AND WATED COMMITTEE .-NSW ENGINE..

The committee reported the trial of the "Benjamin Brown " engine, built by Messrs. Hathorm and Davey,of Leeds. The report was exceedingly satisfactory. The test showed that the pumping power was 19. millions in excess of that guaranteed by the manufacturers, and they are row entitled under the terms-of the contract,to a premium of -424i17. -It was also reported that At the time the tender of Messrs. Hath)rn, Davey, and Co. yas accepted, it was stated by Mr. Brown, the thou chairman of this committee; that the saving on the fuel account alone would pay good interest on capital ex- pended. The actual result is, that the new engine will pump double the quantity of water pumped by the "James Cross" engine without any incrtase M the quantity of fuel. This represents an annual saving in-, the coal bill alone on last year's price of £150,0r 13 per cent, on the cost of the engine and pumps arid 9 6 per cent. on total cost of the whole scheme, i.e., £9,726. In addiaoa to this there will be a large profiksitit the extra ,waterhld. The consumption last month iti'2B days was 89,825,000 gallons, or 96,241,000 gallons for the nonth. This is considerably in excess of any previous record and also of our previous pumping capacity, so that but for the opportune ccinpletion of the new scheme the town would last month have suffered from shortness of water." S.atisfactory progress is being made with the new gasholder tanks at Ditton. The excavation for the tank wall has been completed. The concrete foundation for the wall has been put in; and the wall itself carried up a distance of 4ft., A certificate for £3OO, the amount due on account, is submitted. The illuminating power of the gas during the month has averaged 17 90 candles. It was resolved " That the firemen's cottages be con- nected with the stables, the Town Hall, and the Police Station, by means of electric bells, and that alarm stan- dards be placed in public positions near the Police bta- tion, kc."—Alderman Tiiiimis proposed the adoption of- the minutes, and in doing so congratulated the Corpora- tion upon the acquisition of such an excellent engine as the "Benjamin Brown."—Alderman Warei ng seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were accepted.

div.head: WIDNES CORPORATION WORKIIEN. THE RATE oF WAGES SCENE IN TUE COUNCIL.
div.p: WIDNES CORPORATION WORKIIEN. THE RATE oF WAGES SCENE IN TUE COUNCIL.

At the monthly meeting of the Widnes Town Council held on Tuesday, Councillor Gough, in ac— cordance with the notice of the motion given moved that " the workmen employed 14 the Wid- nes Corporation in the • gas works be paid Union • wages i.e, fitters 365. per week ,and stokers sa. per shift." In moving the motion Councillor Gough first alluded to the conditions under which the men had to work, and he contended that they were by no means well off in that direction. At the present time there was a department in the Gas Works, known as the " Summer shed," which he knew to be about the hottest In the kingdom, and be challenged the engineer to deny It. 1 When he called the attention of the Committee to this he was politely told that there were plenty of worse places to to work in, in Widnes. lie denied that.

With respect to the plumbers, he pointed out that they were paid from 265. to 333. per week. He contended that upon the Engineer's own admission, the Men sm- pioyeci were not legitimate tradesmen but weresimply labourers, and they came there and picked up the busi- ness in a few weeks. He had heard many complaints respecting the defective plumbing/ and fittings and he named an instance when a joint ou a gas pipe had fallen off, shortly after being put in. Such " scamping " work was both dangerous and inconvenient to the rate- payers who paid prices that entitled them to the ser- vices of proper workmen. Be did not know whether that was one of the Committee's methods of making gas profits, but if it was it was a decidedly despicable one. With respect to the stokel.s they wore decidedly under- paid in comparison to stokers employed by other Cor- porations. Ha closed by saying there woe much unfair- ness shown tee men Who knew their work at the gas works, and those who know the least got on best. Alderman Williamson seconded the motion on the grounds that as the labour party had forced the hands of private employers, he thought it was their duty to force the hands of the Corporation into paying the stan- dard rate of wages.

Alderman Timis contended that the wages paid to the workmen were equal to those paid in other towns. , The men were satisfied and no one had a right to inter- fere with them. Ile thought the motion would tend to reate ill-feeling and discontent. Councillor Smith said that a week or two ago Coun- cillor Gough went to the gas works, took off his coat, and worked for half a day with the stokers. He asked if that was not most unbecoming on the part of any member of that Council. It looked to him like the work of an agitator more than the work of a Councillor. klt was a most extraordinary procedure, and discreditable to the Council. Councillor Gough denied that he had, acted as an agitator. He said he went into the works because lie could not get his inforMation otherwise. When he came out he was quietly told by the Chairman that lie would not have to go int* the works again without notifying it at the office. It seemed to him that the inside of these works would not stand looking at under those circumstances. The motion was put to the vote and Inst. Those who voted for it were :—Alderman Tilley, Alderman William- son ,and Councillors Gough,Carney,Singleton,and Quinn.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. SCH OLA RSHIP SCHEME, 'MASSES II AND lII. CLASS ll.—The Cheshire County Council offers for Competition,fiftyScholarships for Science scbjects,thirty- five for Art subjects, and twenty-five for Commercial subjects. These will be tenable at Evening Classes, at Schools approved by the Technical Instruction Commit- tee, for one year ; and are open to students of either sex who are not less than Fourteen years of age, and are resident in the Administrative County. CLASS lll.—The Cheshire County Council also offers for Competition, ten Special Day Scholarships, tenable at Owen's College, Manchester, University College, Liverpool, Technical School, Manchester, or other Institution approved by the Technical Instruction Com- mittee. Candidates must not be less than Sixteen years of age, and resident in the Administrative County. The Scholarships will be granted in the first instance for one year, but may be renewed for a second or third year. Full particulars of the above and forms of application may be obtained from the undersigned. RICHARD P. WARD, Organizing Secretary. Everard Villa, Crewe.
